Mount the car decked with kinsuka-flowers and śalmali-flowers, with all forms, gold-hued, well-turned, fair-wheeled; O Sūryā, ascend the world of immortality and make your wedding-journey pleasant for your husband.
Arise hence, for this woman now has a husband. I entreat Viśvāvasu with homage and with hymns. Seek another woman not yet given in marriage, sitting with her fathers — know that to be your allotted portion from birth.
Arise hence, Viśvāvasu; with obeisance we entreat you. Seek another ripely nubile woman; release this wife to be united with her husband.
May the paths be free of thorns, straight, by which our friends conduct our wooer. May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; may the conjugal bond be easily governed, O gods.

title: Rigveda
text:
I free you from the bond of Varuṇa with which the auspicious Savitṛ bound you. In the womb of ṛta, in the world of good deeds, I place you unharmed together with your husband.
I release her hence, not from yonder — I make her well-bound from yonder. So that here, O Indra, bountiful god, she may be blessed with fine sons and good fortune.
May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you onward in their chariot. Go to your home so that you may be mistress of the house; speak your will in the assembly.
Here may your dear happiness with offspring be fulfilled; be wakeful in this house for the gṛhapati fire. Unite your body with your husband; thus growing old together you shall speak in the assembly.
Dark-red it becomes; the spell attached to the garment is expelled. Her kinsmen prosper; the husband is bound in bonds.
Give away the garment of ill omen; distribute the wealth to the Brāhmaṇas. Let this witchcraft go on its way; may the wife enter her husband as the good one.
The body becomes inauspicious, glittering and dangerous, when the husband covers his own limb with the bride's garment.
The diseases that follow from people to the bride's bright wedding-procession — may the sacrifice-worthy gods drive those back to where they came from.
Let not the lurkers find them, those who lie in wait for the pair of householders. May they pass through the difficult places by easy roads; let all ill-wishers flee away.
This bride is auspicious and blessed — come together and behold her. Having bestowed good fortune upon her, then go your ways home.
This thing is harsh and bitter, rough and poisonous — not fit to eat. Only the Brāhmaṇa who truly knows Sūryā is worthy to conduct the wedding rites.
The binding, the loosening, the cutting apart — these are the forms of Sūryā; the Brāhmaṇa purifies all these.

title: Rigveda
text:
I take your hand for good fortune, that you may grow old with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Puraṁdhi — the gods have given you to me for the household fire.
O Pūṣan, rouse for us the most auspicious woman in whom men plant seed; who opens her thighs willingly for us; in whom we willingly deposit the phallus.
To you first of all they led Sūryā around with the wedding-procession. O Agni, give the wife back to the husbands together with offspring.
Agni has given back the wife along with life and brilliance. May her husband live a long life — a hundred autumns.
Soma first possessed you, the Gandharva possessed you next; Agni was your third husband — your fourth husband is born of men.
Soma gave to the Gandharva, the Gandharva gave to Agni; Agni gave me riches and sons, and this woman here.
Be here; do not be parted from each other; live out your full span of life. Sporting with your sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home.
May Prajāpati generate offspring for us; may Aryaman anoint us for old age together. O you who are of good omen, enter your husband's world; be auspicious to us among bipeds and quadrupeds.
Be of gentle gaze, no slayer of your husband; be kind to our cattle, of good mind, of good splendour; bearing heroes, devoted to the gods, gentle — be auspicious to us among bipeds and quadrupeds.
O bountiful Indra, make this woman blessed with fine sons and good fortune. Place ten sons in her and make the husband the eleventh.
Be a queen before your father-in-law; be a queen before your mother-in-law. Be a queen before your husband's sister; be a queen before your husband's brothers.
May all the gods unite our hearts; may the waters unite our hearts. May Mātariśvan, may Dhātṛ, may Deṣṭrī join our two hearts together.
The soma-pressers flowed forth; they did not honour Indra as god, where Vṛṣākapi, the noble one, made merry in prosperity — my companion. Indra is above all things.

title: Rigveda
text:
You run away, O Indra, beyond Vṛṣākapi's trouble. You find nothing elsewhere for the drinking of Soma. Indra is above all things.
What has this tawny beast Vṛṣākapi done to you, that you are angry at him, O nobleman, because of his prosperous goods? Indra is above all things.
This Vṛṣākapi whom you cherish, O Indra, whom you protect as your favourite — a dog that is boar-hunting will snap at his ear. Indra is above all things.
The ape has damaged my carved, manifest, precious things. I would cut off his head — it would go ill for the evil-doer. Indra is above all things.
No woman sits in a better seat than I; no woman is swifter in the race than I; none is more forward than I; none lifts her thighs higher than I. Indra is above all things.
Yes, dear easily-found mother, it shall be just as you say. My rump, my thigh, my head — I am excited all over. Indra is above all things.
Why, O fair-armed, pretty-fingered, broad-hipped, wide-thighed one — why do you, O wife of the hero, cast hostile glances at our Vṛṣākapi? Indra is above all things.
This scoundrel thinks of me as if I were without a husband. But I am indeed the heroic wife of Indra, companion of the Maruts. Indra is above all things.
In former times the woman went indeed to the assembly and to the joint invocation. The creative heroine, follower of ṛta, the wife of Indra, is exalted. Indra is above all things.
I have heard that Indrāṇī is the most blessed among these women — for her husband never dies of old age. Indra is above all things.
I, Indrāṇī, would not rejoice without my companion Vṛṣākapi, whose dear, moist oblation goes among the gods. Indra is above all things.
O wealthy wife of Vṛṣākapi, blessed with fine sons and fine daughters-in-law — may Indra eat the bulls for you, the dear offering that brings fulfilment. Indra is above all things.

title: Rigveda
text:
For me they cook fifteen and twenty bulls at once. I eat the fat and both my flanks are filled. Indra is above all things.
Like a sharp-horned bull roaring among the herds — O Indra, the pressed draught pleases your heart, which the devoted presser presses for you. Indra is above all things.
He does not prevail in whose thighs the penis dangles. He prevails whose hairy thing opens wide when he sits down. Indra is above all things.
He does not prevail whose hairy thing opens wide when he sits down. He prevails in whose thighs the penis dangles. Indra is above all things.
This Vṛṣākapi, O Indra, has found the slain enemy's wealth: a sword, a new meat-cooking pot, loaded with firewood. Indra is above all things.
I go about observing clearly, distinguishing the Dāsa from the Ārya. I drink of the simple presser's draught, gazing upon the wise one. Indra is above all things.
The desert and the cutting-forest — how many leagues separate them? O Vṛṣākapi, come homeward, come back to the nearer dwellings. Indra is above all things.
Come back again, Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange things well. You who destroy sleep, come back by the path to the home. Indra is above all things.
When you two came home northward, O Indra and Vṛṣākapi — where has that nimble beast gone, who pleased the people of the house? Indra is above all things.
Parśu, a human woman, bore twenty children at one time. Good fortune came indeed to her whose belly bore this pain. Indra is above all things.
I kindle the demon-slaying, powerful Agni; I approach the protection of the most widely renowned friend. Agni, whetted and kindled with sacred rites — may he guard us by day and guard us by night from harm.
O Jātavedas, kindled, with your iron fangs touch the Yātudhānas with your flame. With your tongue seize upon the wicked gods; having cut down the flesh-eaters, place them in your mouth.

title: Rigveda
text:
Set your two deadly fangs, biting both from below and above, O king. And circling through the atmosphere, crush the Yātudhānas with your jaws.
O Agni, having bent your arrows with sacrifices, smearing the sticks with your voice like lightning-bolts — with these pierce the Yātudhānas in the heart; break the backs of their arms.
O Agni, split the skin of the Yātudhāna; your flame like a deadly bolt should smite him. O Jātavedas, shatter his limbs joint by joint; let the flesh-rending flesh-devourer scatter the shreds.
Where now you see him, O Jātavedas, standing or moving, or flying through the atmosphere on its pathways — with your whetted arrow shoot him, O Śarva.
Deliver also the one who has been caught, O Jātavedas, from the Yātudhāna that has seized upon him. O Agni, blazing, strike down the attacker first; let the spotted ewes that devour raw flesh eat him.
Declare here which one it is, O Agni — which Yātudhāna is doing this thing. Seize him with your faggot, O youngest one; deliver him to the sight of the man-seeing one.
With your sharp eye guard the sacrifice, O Agni; lead it forward to the Vasus, O wise one. Blazing against the injurious demons — let not the Yātudhānas deceive you, O man-seeing one.
O man-seeing one, scan the demon about the settlements; shatter the three points of his weapon. O Agni, shear his ribs with your heat; cut the Yātudhāna's root in three places.
Let the Yātudhāna come thrice into your snare — whoever, O Agni, attacks truth with falsehood. Thundering with your flame, O Jātavedas, destroy him openly before the one who praises you.
O Agni, set your eye — the hoof-breaking, revealing eye — with which you see the Yātudhāna. Like Atharvan, with the divine light, burn up the unrecognised one who injures truth.
O Agni, the arrow that is born from the biting of pairs this day, when the chanting ones produce the harsh weapon of voice from wrath of mind — with that arrow pierce the Yātudhānas in the heart.

title: Rigveda
text:
O Agni, sever the Yātudhānas with your heat; sever the demons with your flame. Blazing, sever the wicked gods with your rays; sever the devourers of life.
Today let the gods cut away the crooked one; let the fierce curses turn back upon him. Let the arrows of speech reach the vital spot of the word-thief; let the Yātudhāna come to the snare of all.
The Yātudhāna who compounds himself with human flesh, with horse-flesh, with cattle-flesh; who steals the milk of the unwounded cow — O Agni, cut off their heads with your flame.
Let the Yātudhāna not eat the year-long milk of the cow, O man-seeing one. O Agni, whichever one would swallow the colostrum — pierce that one straight through the vitals with your flame.
Let the Yātudhānas drink the poison of the cows; let the evil-fated ones be cut off for Aditi. Let the god Savitṛ deliver them away; let them win away their portion from the plants.
From of old, O Agni, you have slain the Yātudhānas; the demons have not overcome you in battles. Burn the flesh-eating fools one after another; let them not escape your divine weapon.
O Agni, protect us from below and above, from behind, and guard us from the front as well. Let your ageless, most burning ones, blazing, burn up the evil-speaker.
O king, guard us from behind and in front, from below and above, O seer, with your poet-wisdom. O Agni, friend to the friend, ageless against decay, immortal among us mortals.
O Agni, we set you as a rampart of strength around us — the inspired one, bright-hued day by day, slayer of those who are crooked of will.
With poison burn back the crooked-willed demons, O Agni, with your sharp flame, with your heat-tipped spears.
O Agni, burn back the paired Yātudhānas, the Kimīdins. I sharpen you; be undeceived and wakeful, O inspired one, with sacred thoughts.

title: Rigveda
text:
O Agni, with your heat shear back the heat; sever it on all sides. Break the force and heroic strength of the Yātudhāna demon.
The oblation protected, ageless, heaven-finding, touching the sky, offered and accepted in the fire — for the bearing of that, for the world, for the law, the gods spread out with their self-power.
The world swallowed, hidden by darkness, became manifest in light when Agni was born. At his birth the gods — earth, sky, waters — and the plants rejoiced in his friendship.
Urged on by the sacrifice-worthy gods, I will now praise Agni, the ageless, the great — he who with his radiance stretched out earth, this sky here, and the two worlds, and the atmosphere.
He who was the first Hotṛ, dear to the gods, whom they anointed with ghee as they chose him — Agni Jātavedas made swift both the winged world and the four-footed world.
O Jātavedas, O Agni, when you stood at the top of the world with the shining realm — we praise you with thoughts, hymns, and recitations. Thus you became worthy of sacrifice, filling the two worlds.
Agni becomes the crown of the earth by night; from that the sun is born, rising at dawn. This is the power of those worthy of sacrifice: the water moves swiftly with full understanding.
He who, sky-born, blazing with greatness, shone brilliantly and was worth beholding — into that Agni the self-sustaining gods poured all oblations with the words of the well-spoken hymn.
First and foremost the gods generated the well-spoken hymn, and then Agni, and then the oblation. He became their self-sustaining sacrifice — sky knows him, earth knows him, the waters know him.
The Agni whom the gods generated, into whom they poured all the worlds — he, straightening out with his flame both earth and this sky, warmed them with his greatness.
For with praise the gods in heaven generated Agni, filling the two worlds with his powers. They made him threefold for the world — he cooks the plants of all forms.

title: Rigveda
text:
When the sacrifice-worthy gods placed him in heaven as the solar child of Aditi — when the two moving ones became a pair, then all the worlds saw everything.
For the good of all the world the gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the signal light of days — he who stretches out the shining dawns and removes darkness, going with his flame.
The poet-seers, the sacrifice-worthy gods, generated Agni Vaiśvānara as the imperishable; he who moved, shaking the ancient star — the mighty, great overseer of the sacrifice.
We address with sacred hymns Agni the wise, Vaiśvānara, ever blazing — he who by his greatness encompassed the wide earth, god from below and from above.
I have heard of two paths — of the Fathers and of the gods — and of mortals. By these two paths all this moving world comes together, whatever is between Father Heaven and Mother Earth.
The two that embrace each other carry him who moves, born from the head, comprehended by the mind. He has stood facing all the worlds, without faltering, the swift one, blazing.
Where the lower and the upper speak, of the two sacrificial ones — which one of us two does he know? Friends have reached the common banquet; who can proclaim this sacrifice?
How many fires, how many suns, how many dawns, how many waters are there? I am not speaking controversially to you, O Fathers — I am asking you, O sages, to know.
For as great a measure as the face of the dawn in which the eagle Mātariśvan dwells — to that measure the Brāhmaṇa who comes to the sacrifice, sitting below the Hotṛ, establishes it.
I praise Indra the most manly, by whose greatness the shining realms and the ends of the earth were pushed apart — he who, holding men together, filled the wide spaces, overflowing with his greatness beyond the rivers.
Indra turned the sun around the wide dwelling places like chariot wheels. He smote the dark darkneses with his brilliance, like a flood that stays nothing.

title: Rigveda
text:
Chant for him the unceasing, unturning hymn — the new prayer unlike any in earth or sky. Indra, the noble one, sorted out the births like backs of cattle; he does not rule over a friend.
I send forth songs to Indra like an unrestricted current of waters from the depth of the ocean — he who, like an axle-pin holding the wheels, with his powers propped apart earth and heaven on every side.
His anger has drunk its fill; with triple food he has been nourished; he is the rushing, laborious one, with mace, the soma-drinker. The stalky shrubs and forests — none of the things below have deceived Indra.
Neither heaven and earth, nor desert, nor atmosphere, nor mountains, nor Soma have measured him. When his wrath is stirred, he shatters the solid and breaks the firm things.
He slew Vṛtra like an axe in the forest; he broke the strongholds and dug out the rivers. He split the mountain like a new water jar; Indra freed the cows with his own yoke-fellows.
You, O Indra the wise, cut off that sin-incurring thing; like a sword you sever crooked limb from limb. Those who injure the law of Mitra and Varuṇa injure a friend, as if breaking a yoke-fellow.
Those evil ones who injure Mitra, who injure Aryaman, who injure the compacts, who injure Varuṇa — sharpen your heavy weapon against the enemies, O bull, the red-rayed one that whets itself.
Indra is lord of heaven; Indra is lord of earth; Indra is lord of the waters, of the mountains. Indra is lord of the prosperous, lord of the wise; Indra is to be invoked in peace and in toil.
Indra excels the seasons, the days; he excels the atmosphere, the lap of the ocean. He excels the breadth of the wind, the ends of the earth; he overflows beyond the rivers and the dwelling-places.
Like a blazing signal of the dawns, may your weapon revolve, O Indra, unhindered. Piercing like a stone, hurled down from heaven — with your most burning weapon strike those who are false friends.

title: Rigveda
text:
The months followed him, the forests followed him, the plants followed him, the mountains followed him. The two worlds crying out followed Indra; the waters followed him as he was born.
When, O Indra, will that be perceived of you — that you struck the demon that was destroying the wicked? Those who are hostile to Mitra, like cattle at the slaughtering post — when will they lie fallen, stuck to this earth?
Those hostile enemies that have crept upon us, who swelled as a mighty army — O Indra, let the enemies be engulfed in blind darkness; may the nights rich in good light pour over them.
Truly, many a pressing-rite of peoples exhilarates you; the prayers of the singing seers exhilarate you. Resounding here with help and companioned invocation, pass beyond all who sing hymns and come to us.
Thus may we, O Indra, know you to be of those who enjoy, of those who are newly benevolent. Praising, may we know you at the turning of each day with your help; we are Viśvāmitras, O Indra, even now.
For our welfare may we call upon Maghavan Indra, the most manly in this battle for the prize — the fierce one who hearkens for our aid in conflicts, smiting Vṛtras, conqueror of wealth.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He surrounds the earth on all sides and extends beyond by ten fingers.
This Puruṣa is indeed all this world — what has been and what shall be. And he is lord of immortality, that which grows beyond through food.
Such is his greatness, yet Puruṣa is greater still. One quarter of him is all living beings here; three quarters of him are the immortal in heaven.
Three quarters of the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter here came into being again. From that he stepped forward on all sides, into what eats and what does not eat.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj the Puruṣa was born again. Being born, he extended beyond the earth — both behind and before.

title: Rigveda
text:
When the gods, with the Puruṣa as their oblation, spread out the sacrifice — spring was the melted butter, summer was the firewood, and autumn was the offering.
They consecrated with water on the barhis-grass the Puruṣa born in the beginning. With him the gods sacrificed, and the Sādhyas, and the seers.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the clotted oblation was gathered. He made from it the animals of the air — those of the forest and those of the village.
From that all-offered sacrifice were born the Ṛk-verses and the Sāmans. The metres were born from it; the Yajus was born from it.
From it were born horses, and all creatures with two rows of teeth. Cows were born from it; from it were born goats and sheep.
When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What is his mouth called? What his two arms? What are his two thighs and his two feet called?
His mouth was the Brāhmaṇa; his two arms were made the Rājanya; his two thighs are what the Vaiśya is; from his two feet the Śūdra was born.
The moon was born from his mind; the sun was born from his eye. From his mouth came Indra and Agni; from his breath Vāyu was born.
From his navel came the atmosphere; from his head the sky evolved. From his two feet the earth; from his ear the directions — thus they arranged the worlds.
Seven were its enclosing sticks; thrice seven were the kindling-sticks prepared, when the gods, spreading out the sacrifice, bound the Puruṣa as the sacrificial animal.
With the sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; these were the first cosmic laws. These great ones attained the vault of heaven, where the ancient Sādhya gods dwell.
He is kindled together with the wakeful ones, waxing old in the house, the house-lord quickening at the station of Iḷā; the Hotṛ of all, most worthy of the oblation, all-pervading, radiant — as a true friend he is befriended.

title: Rigveda
text:
He of splendid beauty, a guest in every house, nestles in every forest like a swift hawk; he, the people's own, does not despise any folk, but dwells among the clans — a clansman among every clan.
O Agni, expert among experts by your power of discernment, you are of excellent will; a seer by your wisdom, you know all things. You alone, O treasure among treasures, are lord of whatever Heaven and Earth cherish.
Knowing, O Agni, your timely birthplace — the butter-rich station of Iḷā — you have been set in place; your gleaming rays have become visible, like the dawns, blameless, like the rays of the sun.
Your splendours flash like lightning of the rain-cloud; wondrous, they appear like the banners of the Dawns. When you are sent forth among the plants and forests, you gather your own food into your mouth.
Him — Agni — the plants bore as their timely embryo; him the waters, like mothers, brought forth; him, ever the same one, the trees and herbs, those pregnant and those giving birth, perpetually deliver.
Fan-fanned by the wind, impelled, you spread yourself following the dry fuel, flashing swiftly through the food; your un-aging hosts rush at you separately, like charioteers, O Agni, blazing.
Agni the author of wisdom, the adornment of the assembly, the Hotṛ, most pre-eminent, most inspired — him alone they choose for the small oblation, and him alone they choose for the great sacrifice — none other than you.
You alone they choose here, the devotees of you, O Agni, as Hotṛ among the wise in the assemblies; when the god-worshipping Manus, possessing oblations, with trimmed grass-strewings, lay down offerings before you.
Yours, O Agni, is the office of Hotṛ; yours, seasonally, that of Potṛ; yours is the role of Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnīdh for the truth-striving; yours is the Praśāstṛ's part; you act as the Adhvaryu, and you are also the Brahmán and the householder in our home.

title: Rigveda
text:
Whatever mortal, O Agni, for immortality's sake presents you with fuel or with the making of oblation — for him you become the Hotṛ, you go on the messenger's errand, you address him, you sacrifice, you perform the adhvara.
These thoughts, these words from us, these hymns, praises, and songs of eulogy have assembled together for him, desiring wealth, for Vasu, for Jātavedas — he who grows by each increase and who has delighted in them.
This newest eulogy I would speak for the Ancient one, who yearns — let him hear us. May it touch deeply within his heart, like a well-dressed, loving wife close to her husband.
For him in whom horses, bulls, oxen, cows, and rams are released and offered as oblations — for the drinker of sweet drink, for the Soma-backed wise one — I generate from my heart a beautiful hymn for Agni.
O Agni, the oblation is to be placed in your mouth — clarified butter as in the ladle, Soma as in the pressing-bowl. Grant us a prize-winning wealth, with excellent heroes, famed and glorious, and great.
I praise for you the chariot-driver of the sacrifice, the lord of the peoples, the Hotṛ of the nights, the guest rich in light; blazing, roaring upon the dry tawny ones, the virile one, the banner-fire, the adorable, has stretched himself across the sky.
Both groups — gods and mortals — have made him the universal one, Agni, the establishing law of the assembly, its practitioner; like the ancient night of the Dawns, the purohita, Tanūnapāt of the ruddy one, they lick him.
We celebrate his leadership and also the merchants' thought; his branches, well-offered, are for eating. When the terrible ones have attained immortality, they revolve perpetually then among the divine folk.
For Heaven, the wide expanse, is the outlet of Ṛta; the great Aramati is the more wondrous worship; Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa have recognised each other, and also Bhaga and Savitṛ who bestows pure power.

title: Rigveda
text:
With Rudra the rapid one, the rivers flow onward; they have run across the great Aramati. By those with whom the encircler roams the wide expanse, roaring everywhere, he sprinkles everything in his belly.
Active, the Rudras, the Maruts of all peoples, the eagles of the sky, the nestlings of the Asura — together with them Varuṇa surveys, and Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra with the swift gods, himself swift.
Those who have toiled have reached their enjoyment in Indra — the hero in his aspect, and the bulls in their virility. The skilled singers who now have fashioned his fitting token, the companion-bolt, for the seats of men.
Even the sun's tawny mares have been held back by him; who from Indra the mightier does not fear? From the belly of the fearful bull the mighty roar thunders day by day, unhindered.
Aim today with homage a hymn for Rudra the able, the lord of heroes; through whose benevolent, self-luminous swift ones he pursues the sky according to desire, of his own fame.
They have spread fame far for offspring — Bṛhaspati the bull, the Soma-kindred ones; Atharvan by sacrifices first sustained them; the gods and the Bhṛgus have come together through their powers.
Indeed Heaven and Earth with their abundant seed, Narāśaṁsa of four forms, Yama, Aditi, the god Tvaṣṭṛ, Draviṇodas, Ṛbhukṣan — the Maruts and Viṣṇu have honoured both worlds.
And let that far-famed seer of the Uśijas, Ahi Budhnya, hear our invocation; let the Sun and Moon roaming the sky, dwellers in heaven, both understand this sacrifice by their wisdom — Nahuṣī among the workers.
May Pūṣan of all the gods further our journey; may Apāṁ Napāt protect for the offering; sing the self-sustaining Wind with better songs — you two Aśvins, easy to invoke, hear this at your going.
Him, the lord of these fearless peoples, self-glorious, we praise with songs; Aditi along with all the divine women, un-assailed — the young lord of heroes, the night's master.

title: Rigveda
text:
Here the ancient Aṅgiras sang from birth; the pressing-stones raised high look upon the rite; through which the far-seer gained the sky, the path is firm, the self-sharpened axe at work in the wood-bearing one.
Be great and wide for us, O Heaven and Earth, like two young women, the two great Rodases always with us; protect us with them from the powerful, protect us with them in battle.
That mortal in every sacrifice serves the gods — he who, with good thoughts, the most far-famed, approaches them with homage.
The generosity of all the gods is the best great gift; for the All-gods, mighty all of them, are all worthy of sacrifice at every sacrifice.
Those kings of immortality — the delightful ones — Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa the encircler; where is Rudra, lauded of men; the Maruts, Pūṣan, Bhaga?
And by night, both rich in bull-power — Sun and Moon, home-companions, for our dwelling; when Ahi Budhnya settles among these at the foundations, primordial.
And may the two divine Aśvins, lords of beauty, and Mitra-Varuṇa with their forms protect us widely; he reaches great wealth — passing over difficulties as if a desert.
And may even the Rudras be gracious to us, the Aśvins, all the gods, the lord of the chariot, Bhaga; Ṛbhu, Vāja, Ṛbhukṣan, the encircler, the all-knowing ones.
Ṛbhu, Ṛbhukṣā, Ṛbhu — the joy of the devout; your two bay coursers, O swift-running one; whose chant alone is hard to surpass, whose sacrifice is set apart from all human ones.
Make us blameless, divine Savitṛ — he who is praised among the lords of bounty; like Indra with the carriers, he has rolled the wheel of these clans like a rein.
Set for us, O Heaven and Earth, joy among our heroes — fame perceived by all peoples; strength for winning the prize, strength also for overcoming wealth in the contest.
This praise, O mighty Indra who yearns for us, wherever it may be, protect for victory; protect always for victory — may the joyous one find it, O Vasu.

title: Rigveda
text:
This hymn of mine, stretched out as a cord in the sun, shining day by day, men have made grow; it is a charm for concord, not horse-like, carved like a carpenter's work, unshaken.
He has turned toward those whose wealth is yoked together — golden wealth; not weakened in mind, not unmanly, not extended uselessly as though spread about in vain.
That I would proclaim for Duḥśīman, Pṛthavāna, and Vena; I would proclaim it for Rāma among the powerful asuras — those who, for the harnessing, possess five hundred attendants — may their path be renowned.
Here indeed I have perceived seventy and seven; Tānva shone forth at once, Pārthya shone forth at once, Māyava shone forth at once.
Let them speak forth; we shall speak too — to the pressing-stones from those that speak, to those that speak. When the rocks, the mountains together, swift ones, carry the resonance and sound, O Soma-bearers, to Indra.
These speak a hundredfold, a thousandfold; they cry out with their tawny mouths; the pressing-stones stretched out, well-wrought by their good craft, first eagerly eat even the Hotṛ's food.
These speak out; they have found honey for the bowl; they swing down upon the cooked raw flesh. They — the bulls, gleaming-toothed — cried out eagerly while devouring the branch of the ruddy tree.
They speak greatly, gladdened by the intoxicant, crying out; they have found honey for the bowl of Indra, the gladdening one; the wise ones, clasping one another, leaping with their sisters, have made the earth resound with their stamps.
The fair-winged ones, the black, lively ones, made speech in the air-hole of the nether stone; they guide downward the product of the upper stone; the sun-white ones have deposited abundant seed.
Like fierce ones flowing forth they came together, yoked bulls bearing the yoke together; as they breathed and swallowed they cried out — you can hear the neighing of them like that of horses.

title: Rigveda
text:
Ten coursers, ten girths, ten yoke-ropes, ten distances, ten reins — praise the un-aging ones; ten shafts, ten harnessed ones that carry.
These rocks, ten-controlled, swift — their support goes around adorable; they indeed have partaken of the first milky sap of the pressed Soma shoot, the Soma plant.
They, the Soma-drinkers, lick Indra's two bays; milking the shoot they sit upon the cow. By what is milked by them — having drunk the Soma-sweet honey — Indra grows, expands, exerts himself as a bull.
The shoot is your bull — you shall not indeed be harmed, O praise-possessing ones, always feeding from the bowl; with the majesty of one rich in gifts you are lovely — you whose pressing-stones have served the sacrifice.
With holes, without holes — these rocks are unwearied, unloosened, immortal; not ailing, not aging, all-pervading by their power, well-rounded, never thirsty, unborn of thirst.
Firm, like your fathers age after age, desiring safety, they do not yoke to the seat; ever-young, swallowing tawny ones, of tawny colour, they have resounded to heaven and earth with their cry.
That the rocks speak out at the unharnessing as on the journey — like drinkers of the ointment, indeed, with their thumps; sowing seed like grain-workers, they mix the Soma but do not diminish it in their devouring.
At the pressed sacrifice they have made speech over it — playing ones, striking like a mother; release the thought of those that have pressed well; let the stones revolve as they resound.
O wife, linger a while with me in heart, O terrible one; let us now mingle our words together. These our mutual counsels, once spoken, will not bring happiness on another day beyond.
What shall I do with this speech of yours? I have stepped forth like the foremost of the dawns. O Purūravas, go back home again; I am as hard to catch as the wind.

title: Rigveda
text:
Like an arrow from the quiver shot for beauty, winning cattle, swift as a hundred — in the will of the powerless one they flashed, but the shakers did not notice the bleat of the ewe.
She who brings treasure — providing sustenance to the father-in-law — O Uṣas, if she desires a home close by; she has reached the home where she took delight, pierced day and night by one of reed.
Three times a day the Vaitasena would strike me, and you would fill me also insatiably; I came after your sign, O Purūravas — you were a king among heroes, the soul of my body.
Those well-adorned ones, in rows, winning favour, their eyes like a lake — roaming, not knotted — those tawny anointings have flowed; like cows and milk-cows they have lowed for beauty.
Together with this one being born, the divine women sat — and the self-welcome rivers made him grow; when, O Purūravas, for great joy, the gods made you grow for the slaying of the Dasyus.
When a human man dwells among those non-human ones, leaving his cloak among them; like Bhujyu flying away from me — they trembled, those touching the chariot, like horses.
When a mortal intermingles with the immortal ones and does not combine his deeds with theirs; those flowing ones adorn their own bodies — like biting horses, they play.
She who flashed like a darting lightning, bringing to me the things I yearn for, close to the waters — a hero was born, well-born; let Urvaśī extend long life.
You were born indeed for protection; you have placed that strength in me, O Purūravas. I, knowing, instructed you on that very day; you did not listen to me — what do you say you have not enjoyed?
When will the son, being born, seek his father? He will shed tears, knowing. Who would separate a couple of one mind, when Agni shines among the parents-in-law?
I will speak in answer — the tear rolls — he shall not weep like a wheel for an auspicious wife; I shall send you forth that which belongs to you among us — go home, O fool, do not perish.

title: Rigveda
text:
The god-blessed one today may rush off, not returning, to go to the remotest distance; then he would lie in the lap of Nirṛti — then the fierce wolves would devour him.
O Purūravas, do not die; do not fall; let not the un-gracious wolves devour you; there are truly no friendships with women — the hearts of these are the hearts of jackals.
When, changed in form, I lived among mortals, spending the nights through four autumns, eating a drop of ghee once a day — it is with this satisfaction that I still wander thus.
I, Vasiṣṭha, seek to learn from Urvaśī who fills the atmosphere, who measures the realm of space. May the gift of good deeds stand near you — turn back; my heart is burning.
Thus these gods say to you, O son of Iḷā, even as you are here a kinsman of death: your offspring shall sacrifice to the gods with oblation, and you yourself shall also rejoice in heaven.
For you, great one, at the assembly I have proclaimed your two bays; I have praised to the worshipper your beautiful, bay-coloured joy; you who shed welcome clarified butter with your bays — may my songs enter into you of bay form.
Those who with one voice together urge the bay toward the bay womb, as toward the heavenly seat; whom the milk-cows fill as with the bays — sing to Indra the bay-possessing might.
His bolt is tawny, of iron; tawny is his desire, tawny in his two fists; radiant, fair-jawed, with tawny-anger dart — in Indra the tawny forms have been instilled.
Like a banner in the sky the bay one has been set; the tawny bolt has spread like swift arrows; the iron, bay-jawed one who smote the serpent became he who bears the bay — with a thousand flames.
You, ever you, O bay-maned Indra, are praised, worshipped by former sacrificers; you love bay things, all praise is yours — the ungiven bounty of the bay-born, the lovely one.

title: Rigveda
text:
The two lovely bays carry in the chariot Indra, the wielder of the bolt, the glad, the laudable joy; many pressings are lovely for him — the Soma-bays have run for Indra.
The bays have run fit for desire; urging the steady one, the two swift bays go; he who goes with pleasure with the bay coursers — he has reached his bay-coloured desire.
Bay-bearded, bay-maned, iron, at the quick draft he who is a bay-drinker has grown; he whose two bays with prize-winning wealth in coursers — may he pass beyond all difficulties.
Whose two tawny jaws flew up like ladles, the two tawny ones flashing for the prize; when having drunk of the lovely intoxicating juice, the two bays polished the made bowl.
And the dwelling of the lovely one in the folds echoed — the bay-possessing one shouted for the prize like a racing horse; for the great power-goddess longed for it by force; you have placed great sustenance from the lovely one.
Filling both worlds by your greatness, O one delighted by bays, you love ever-new beloved hymns; make manifest the lovely dwelling of the cow, O Asura, for bay Sūrya.
Let the impellers of men carry you, bay-delighted, on your chariot, bay-jawed Indra; drink, as you love it, of the brought mead — loving the sacrifice, at the common joy feast, at the ten-fold pressing.
You have drunk of the former pressings, O bay-possessing one; now this pressing is entirely yours; drink the sweet Soma, O Indra — O bull, fill yourself completely in your belly.
The plants that were born of old, three ages before the gods — I shall meditate upon the hundred and seven abodes of those tawny ones.
A hundred are your abodes, O mothers, a thousand your growths; make this man of mine free from disease, you of a hundred powers.
Rejoice, O plants, you that are flowering and fruitful; like mares that conquer together, the herbs, those that carry across.

title: Rigveda
text:
O plants, you who are mothers — the divine ones — I invoke you as such; may I gain a horse, a cow, a garment — and your own life-force, O man.
Your resting place is in the Aśvattha tree, your dwelling has been made in the Parṇa leaf; you are truly sharers in cattle when you win the man.
Where the plants have assembled like kings in a council — that inspired one is called a healer, a slayer of demons, a dispeller of disease.
I have found all the plants — those rich in horses, rich in Soma, enlivening, full of vigour — for his uninjured well-being.
The vigours of the plants go up like cows from the cow-pen; those that shall win wealth — and your own self, O man.
Your mother is called Iṣkṛti, and you are the cleansers; you are the running ones, the wing-bearing ones — what ails, you cleanse away.
Beyond all enclosures they have stepped like a thief toward the fold; the plants have shaken loose whatever ailment afflicts the body.
When I, quickening these, take the plants in my hand — the soul of the disease perishes, as if before a life-snatcher.
Into whose every limb, every joint, you plants spread — drive out the consumption from him, like a fierce lion resting in the middle.
O consumption, fly away together with the blue jay and the spotted one; fly away with the rush of the wind, together with the downward swoop — perish.
Let one of you help another; let each one aid the next; all of you in agreement — help this my speech.
Those that bear fruit and those without fruit, those without flowers and those that flower — prompted by Bṛhaspati, may they free us from distress.
May they free me from the curse, and from Varuṇa's bond; from Yama's noose as well, and from all divine transgression.
Flying down, the plants have spoken all around from the sky: that man whom we reach while he is living, he shall not be harmed.

title: Rigveda
text:
O you who are the plants, ruled by Soma, many and hundred-eyed — among them you are the highest; I have given you gladly for desire, wholesome to the heart.
You plants ruled by Soma, spread all over the earth, prompted by Bṛhaspati — grant your power to this one.
Let not the digger be harmed — he for whom I dig you; may all of ours, two-footed and four-footed, be free from disease.
Those who hear this nearby and those who have come from afar — all the herbs coming together, grant your power to this one.
The plants speak together with Soma the king: O king, we shall carry across the one for whom the Brahmin prepares us.
You are the highest, O plant; your props are the trees; let him who would oppress us become a prop — a dependent of ours.
O Bṛhaspati, meet the deity on my behalf — whether you be Mitra or Varuṇa or Pūṣan; or whether you be together with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, with the Maruts — let him send rain for Śaṃtanu.
O Devāpi, a divine, swift, wise messenger has come to me from you; turn yourself facing toward me; I place a bright speech in your mouth.
Set a bright, disease-free, active speech in our mouths, O Bṛhaspati; with which we may win rain for Śaṃtanu — the sweet drop has entered from the sky.
Let the sweet drops come to us, O Indra; give us a thousand above the chariot; sit down to the Hotṛ's task, sacrifice in due order, serve the gods with oblation, O Devāpi.
Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, the Ṛṣi, sitting in the Hotṛ seat; Devāpi, seeking the goodwill of the gods — he directed the celestial rain-waters from the upper toward the lower sea.
In this upper sea the waters held back by the gods had stood still; they ran, released by Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, sent forth by Devāpi — upon the oblation-sprinkled ones.
When Devāpi, appointed purohita for Śaṃtanu, having been chosen for the Hotṛ's office, blazed with compassion — Bṛhaspati, bestowing what the gods hear, what wins rain, gave him speech.

title: Rigveda
text:
You, O Agni, whom Devāpi, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa the human, blazing, has kindled — praised along with all the gods — send forth rain-bringing Parjanya.
The ancient seers came to you with their hymns; all of them at the rites, O much-invoked one; among us are thousands beyond the chariots — come to our sacrifice, O you with red-roan steeds.
O Agni, ninety-nine oblations beyond the chariot, thousands, have been offered to you; with them grow in many bodies, O hero — impelled, release the rain from the sky for us.
O Agni, present these ninety thousand together as the share for Indra the bull; knowing the paths seasonally trodden by the gods, place Aulāna among the gods in the sky.
O Agni, drive away the destroyers, drive away the hard-to-conquer; drive away disease, drive away the demons; from this great sea of the sky send the fullness of waters to us here.
What wonder do you impel for us, O wise one, to make the far-reaching cry grow? What at the dawning of his might shall he bestow? He shaped the bolt, the Vṛtra-slayer, he swelled it with power.
For he advances with lightning's flash pursuing the chant; by his asura-power he has sat in the broad womb; he, overpowering with nestlings, without the tricks of the seventh brother of his.
He went for the prize; making ill-footed ones good-footed, the sun-winner sat down going to win; un-rivalled when he found the wealth of the hundred-shafted one — the phallus-gods he smote, he overpowered with his form.
He, the swift bull, pours into the great rivers, into the cows — running foremost in contests; where the footless, chariotless ones are yoked, the trough-horses set the ghee in motion.
He, with the Rudras who bar evil, skilled, having left his home, came to the blameless; I believe that the two insects uncovered coupled, having seized food, causing it to ascend through plunder.

title: Rigveda
text:
The lord, having given the loud-roaring Dāsa, the six-eyed, three-headed one, subdued him; Trita, now strengthened by his strength, struck the boar with his iron-tipped spear.
He, with upraised arrow, shot a dart for the man who injures — against the tormenter; he, the most manly, Nahuṣa, well-born among us, broke open the forts in worthy Dasyu-slaying.
He, like a cloud finding pasture and water, found the way to dwelling, not for us; when the Soma-drop settled with his body — the hawk, Ayopāṣṭi, strikes the Dasyus.
He who grew in power through his mighty acts gave Śuṣṇa to Kutsa in the miser's place; this one led the celebrated seer — he who is the winner of the cloak and of men.
This one, worshipping with his manly helpers, the wonder-worker like Varuṇa with the gods, the magician; this young one, the time-observant, is found — he who measured out the four-footed, restless one.
By his hymns, Ṛjiśvā the Auśija burst open the fold with Pipru's bull; when the adorable Soma-presser made his song shine, he advanced, becoming manifest in his form.
Thus, O Asura, for the growth of the great one, the ant has crept up to Indra on his feet; he going thus shall make well-being for him — food, vigour, good dwelling, all-illumining.
O Indra, hold firm, O bountiful one — only so great an enjoyment; praised here, you who drink the pressed Soma well, be for our growth; let Savitṛ further our famous prayer with the gods — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Carry well the seasonally due share for the bearer; forth to Vāyu, the pure drinker, for the cry of desire; he who has obtained the drinking of the Gaura's milk — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
May the god Savitṛ send us life-force to the straight-going sacrificer who presses Soma; so that we may serve the gods like the simple-hearted — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.

title: Rigveda
text:
May Indra be benevolent to us always; may King Soma come over to us for our well-being; just as they have joined together what belongs to Mitra — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Indra with his recitation and strength has been established before; O Bṛhaspati, you are the extender of life-span; the sacrifice is Manu, Pramati is our dear father — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Indra's divine strength of well-doing; Agni in the house, the praising wise seer; may the sacrifice become the most beautiful delight in the assembly — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
We have not done much wrong in secret, no offence manifest to you, O Vasus, O gods; let no deity through the form of untruth — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Savitṛ has sent disease downward; the rocks drive away what is wider downward; where the pressing-stone is called the great Soma-sweeter — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Let the pressing-stone stand upright, O Vasus, for the presser; keep all hatreds far away; may that god Savitṛ, the praiseworthy protector, be for us — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Let the cows eat vigour and fat in the pasture; you who touch the treasure in the seat of Ṛta — let the body's medicine belong to the body — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
The will-sustaining singer has always been sheltered by Indra alone — the good Pramati of the Soma-pressers; whose streams are the full heavenly udder — we choose Aditi, the all-encompassing.
Wondrous is your brilliance, your victory that fills the will; there are irresistible rivals that fill the praise; by the straightest course, by the right, toward cattle, toward the cow — the eager worshipper strives to surpass all.
Awake, O companions of one mind; kindle Agni together, ye many who are gathered as one. I invoke for your protection Dadhikrā, Agni, and the divine Dawn, and the Indra-aided ones.

title: Rigveda
text:
Make your thoughts glad; stretch out the oar-propelled ship that crosses over; fit the quiver, make ready the weapons; lead forward the sacrifice eastward, O companions.
Yoke the ploughs, spread out the yokes; sow the seed here in the prepared womb. May our hymn and the hearing be fruitful; may the sickle come to the ripened grain all the sooner.
The wise yoke the ploughs and spread the yokes apart one by one; the steadfast ones are gracious toward the gods.
Make the ladles ready; bind the harness-straps together; we will pour into the water-trough that is full, that pours well, inexhaustible.
The trough prepared with ladles, having a good harness-strap, pouring well—I pour into the water-filled, inexhaustible.
Delight the horses; conquer the well-placed prize; make the chariot that bears good fortune. Pour into the wooden-ladle trough, the stone-wheeled, the shoulder-strap-quiver one—the guardian of men.
Build the cattle-pen, for it is your guardian; stitch together armour, broad and wide; build iron, invincible fortresses before you; let not the cup overflow—make it firm.
Turn your sacred thought toward protection; let the gods here worship the divine, sacrifice-worthy one. May she who goes to the pasture like a cow yield to us with a thousand streams the milk of the great cow.
Now pour in the Soma here in the lap of the wooden door; let the stone tools shape it; embrace it with ten girths; yoke the carrier to both shafts.
The carrier, pressing hard upon both shafts, moves within them like one born of two mothers. Erect the tree of the forest in the forest; dig and set the spring.
O men, lift up the phallus, the foremost one; urge it forward, dig for the winning of the prize. Shaking the son from the womb, bring Indra here with pressure to drink the Soma.
May Indra boldly protect your chariot that is well-paired; O much-invoked one, protect us in this contest worthy of fame, in the seizure of prizes.

title: Rigveda
text:
The wind blows up the garment of this woman who won a thousand from the chariot. Mudgalānī became the charioteer in the cow-race; Indrasenā divided the prize won in the battle.
Hold back the bolt, O Indra, within your grasp against those who wish to slay, against those who attack; O bounteous one, drive far away the blow of the Dāsa or the Ārya.
Exultingly he drank the pond of water; shaking he strikes the peak and goes against the foe; the scrotal-load-bearer, seeking renown, stretching out his arms quick to the field, striving.
Lowing, they came up to him; they made the bull urinate in the midst of the race. With him Mudgala won in the final contest a hundredfold, a thousandfold of cattle.
The bull was yoked to the Kakardave; his charioteer, the long-haired Keśī, drove it. The blows of the running bull dragging the cart fall upon Mudgalānī as she sits.
Knowing it, he knocked out the wheel-felly and here he helped, joining the shaft-piece, seeking to aid. Indra lifted up the lord of the unslayable cows; the hump-necked bull hastened with swift feet.
The braided-haired one moved prosperously through the goad; the wood was being fastened to the strap. Performing manly deeds for the many people, watching over the cows, he acquired strengths.
See this yoke-fellow of the bull lying in the middle of the course, the wooden block; by means of him Mudgala won a hundredfold, a thousandfold of cattle in the battles.
Far away the sins—who ever saw it happen thus? They yoke him and then unharness him too. They bring him neither grass nor water; yet the superior one draws the shaft time and again, as one pointing the way.
Like an abandoned wife she understood her husband; swelling, pouring like water from a bent wheel. In this very racing-chariot let us conquer; let the winning be auspicious and lucky.

title: Rigveda
text:
You, O Indra, are the eye of all the world, the eye among eyes. You are the bull; you urge on the bull-pair to seize the race, goading them with the castrated one as yokefellow.
Swift, whetted, terrible like a bull, striker upon striker, shaker of peoples, the battle-shouter, ever-wakeful, sole hero—Indra conquered a hundred armies together.
Conquer with him, the battle-shouter, the unwinking, the victorious, the battle-crying, the hard-to-shake, the bold one; withstand that with Indra, O men—with the arrow-holding bull.
He with arrow-bearers, he with quiver-wearers is master, joined in battle with Indra and his troop. The conqueror in close combat, the Soma-drinker, mighty in arms, with terrible bow, shooting with arrows fitted to the string.
O Bṛhaspati, drive around with your chariot, driving away the Rākṣasas and enemies; breaking armies, crushing in battle, conquering—be the protector of our chariots.
Known by his strength, firm, pre-eminent in heroism, powerful, strong, enduring, terrible; mighty over heroes, bold in battle, born of power—mount the victorious chariot, O Indra, finder of cows.
The breaker of cow-pens, the finder of cows, the thunderbolt-armed, conquering in the course, crushing with might—let the kinsmen follow him in heroism; embrace Indra closely, O companions.
Plunging mightily into the cow-pens, unhurt, the hero of hundredfold wrath—Indra, hard to shake, conqueror of armies, not to be defeated in battle—let him protect our army in the combat.
Let Indra be the leader of these, Bṛhaspati on the right, the sacrifice advance, Soma in front; let the Maruts go at the head of the divine armies that overwhelm and conquer.
The war-cry of Indra the bull, of Varuṇa the king, of the Ādityas, of the terrible host of Maruts—of the great-spirited, world-shaking, conquering gods—has arisen.

title: Rigveda
text:
Exhilarate the weapons, O bounteous one; exhilarate the spirits of my warriors; let the strengths of the prize-winners rise up, O Vṛtra-slayer; let the war-cries of the conquering chariots go forth.
May Indra be with our banners in the encounters; let those arrows of ours conquer; may our heroes be supreme; and do you, O gods, protect us in our calls.
Beguiling the minds of those enemies, seize their limbs, O Apvā, and pass through; advance upon them, burn them with pain in their hearts; let the foes be joined by the blinding darkness.
Go forward, O men, conquer; may Indra grant you shelter. May your arms be terrible and irresistible, as indeed you are.
The Soma has been pressed for you, O much-invoked Indra; come quickly with your two bay horses to the sacrifice. For you the songs of the inspired heroes speed forward; O unconquerable Indra, drink of the pressed juice.
Drink here of what has been purified in the waters, O bay-horsed one; fill your belly with what is pressed by men. The stones have mixed it for you, O Indra; grow strong on them, you who carry the hymn.
I urge you, O bull, to the true foremost drinking—for the outpouring of the pressed juice for you, O bay-horsed one. Delight yourself here, O Indra, with the melodies, with all thoughts, being praised by your might.
With your protection, O lord of might, laying hold of strength by your valour—the eager ones, knowers of the sacred order—they stood exulting in the house of Manu, praising you with progeny, O Indra.
By your leaderships, O bay-horsed one, of you the well-praised, the benevolent, the widely shining—the peoples, holding on to the most bounteous help, spread out as your praisers, O Indra, with your true words.
Come with your two bay horses to the prayers, O bay-horsed one, to drink of the pressed Soma. O Indra, the sacrifice has found you patient; you are the foremost knower of the oblation.

title: Rigveda
text:
Songs adorn the one of a thousand prizes, the overpowerer of aggressors, the good leader, the bounteous, the well-hymned—the unconquered Indra; they marvel at him with reverence, the singers.
The seven divine waters, clear, unblended—with which you crossed the river, O Indra, fort-breaker—ninety streams and nine more flowing: you found the path for gods and for man.
You freed the great waters from the curse; the one god was awake over them. O Indra, with those waters with which you performed the conquest of Vṛtra, may you nourish your body, giving universal life.
Indra the heroic, the resolve, the well-proclaimed—and the melody seeks the much-invoked one. He shattered Vṛtra and made space; the Mighty One, the vanquisher, has overcome the armies.
We call for our welfare the bounteous Indra, the most manly in this battle at the winning of the prize—the one who listens, the terrible, for our protection in combats, the slayer of Vṛtras, the gatherer of riches.
When, O good lord, will the praise you love come to you? The blade will stop—for the long-pressed Soma waiting for the wind to dry it.
He whose two bay horses are well-yoked, going different ways like birds, following their impulse according to their tails—both long-maned like coursers—the lord has given.
From the two Indra removes evil; no mortal who has exerted himself is afraid—when the mighty one has yoked for beauty.
Together with the two, Indra ploughed and ploughed again—of two carts serving together—of two streams going separate ways: the hero, Indra.
He who stood upon the two long-maned ones, wide-stretching, not for nourishment—he wins with his cheek-pieces, like one with strong cheeks.
He of lofty strength proclaimed; the hero fashioned with lofty ones by might—like Ṛbhu in designs, like Mātariśvan.
He who made the thunderbolt for the good smiting of the Dasyu—the golden-maned one, with golden mane—of unwounded jaw, wondrous as the bright space.

title: Rigveda
text:
Sharpen away our sins with the hymn; we who sing hymns would beat down the unsinging. No non-Brahman, no sacrifice thrives separately from you.
When your triple fire stood erect in the dwellings at the shafts of the sacrifice—in unison with the self-glorious ship of the two companions.
May the dappled one be for your glory an over-pourer; may the spotless ladle be for your glory—with which you pour upward into your own cup.
Whether it was a hundred, O lordly one, that Sumitrā praised you thus or that Durmitra praised you thus—when you helped in the slaying of Dasyus the son of Kutsa, when you helped in the slaying of Dasyus the calf of Kutsa.
Both of you now seek that very thing; you spread your thoughts like weavers at their work. Going forth together you have started us onward; like refreshment on a fair day you weave us close.
You rest like camels among the horses; you go like a swift course over the instructed. For you are like messengers of renown among the peoples; do not stay away from us like a buffalo from the drinking-place.
Come together yoked, like the two wings of a bird, like wonderfully varied beasts with the oblation. Blazing like fire for the two divine ones, ranging about, you two worship in many places.
Be our intimate friend—like a father to a son, like a great one with splendour for swiftness, like wind for nourishment, like a ray for enjoyment—come to our call, as one eager to listen.
Like the shaft-joint of the Pūṣan-chariot, pair of pods; like Mitra in truth, hundred-rayed, a hundred-winged; dwelling aloft with strength at a prize like the Gharma-fire; worshipping like a ram, seeking fulfillment.
Swiftly moving like a sickle, swift-going pair; swift-going, flickering like a naitośa creeper; conquering like water-born ones, the two exhilarating ones—those two, Jarāyu and the undecaying Marāyu, for me.

title: Rigveda
text:
Like the Pajras, the love-lorn Marāyu goes round and round; fierce like a sharp blade you two traverse the transactions. Like the offspring of the Ṛbhus, swift-striding of rough gait, fluttering like the wind, ruling over riches.
Like the Gharma-vessel with honey in the belly, the two old ones—the swift-going Bhagavitā pours abundantly; wandering like birds with silvery adornment, mind-adorned, mind-going, not going hither.
Like tall ones you find footing in deep places; like a foot you cross the ford in the assembly. Like an ear you remember the instruction—yes; give us bright wealth, like a portion.
You two send forth honey like the Āraṅgara plant; like a bee in the cow downward-armed; dripping with sweat like a kīnāra worm, you two follow with strength from the good grass-land, as from an arid soil.
May we succeed with our hymn of praise, may we win the prize; come to our chant here together on the chariot. Like fame, like ripe honey among the cows—fulfil the desire of the Aśvins, O share of what comes to be.
Great generosity of these patrons became manifest; all living things were released from darkness. The great light given by the fathers has come; the broad path of the Dakṣiṇā has been seen.
The givers of the Dakṣiṇā stood high in heaven; those who gave horses—they stood with the sun. The givers of gold partake of immortality; the givers of garments, O Soma, extend their life.
The divine fulfilment, the Dakṣiṇā of the god-worship, belongs not to the greedy—for they do not give. But then the men of stretched-forth Dakṣiṇā, fearing blame, the many give.
Those who see men look upon the hundred-streamed wind, the hymn, the finder of heaven, as an oblation. Those who give and bestow at the assembly—they milk the Dakṣiṇā with its seven mothers.
The one who has Dakṣiṇā goes first when invoked; the one with Dakṣiṇā, the village leader, goes in front. Him alone I regard as the king of peoples—who first set the Dakṣiṇā in motion.

title: Rigveda
text:
Him alone they call the Ṛṣi, him the Brahman—the sacrificial Sāma-singer, the reciter of hymns. He knows the three bodies of the Bright One, who first prospered through the Dakṣiṇā.
The Dakṣiṇā gives the horse, the Dakṣiṇā gives the cow; the Dakṣiṇā gives the moon and also gold. He who is the soul wins food through the Dakṣiṇā; the knowing one makes the Dakṣiṇā his armour.
The generous patrons have not died nor gone to lowliness; the generous are not harmed, nor do they waver. This all, whatever this whole world and heaven—all this is given to those who give the Dakṣiṇā.
The generous won the fragrant womb first; the generous won the bride who is well-dressed. The generous won the inner draught of the Surā; the generous won—those who go without being invited.
For the generous one they groom the swift horse; for the generous one the maiden adorns herself sitting. The home of the generous is like a lotus pool, adorned, wondrous like one esteemed by the gods.
Horses with well-carrying loads carry the generous one; the well-wheeled chariot of the Dakṣiṇā rolls. The gods protect the generous in battles; the generous one is the conqueror of foes in the clash of armies.
What desiring has Saramā approached to this place? For the path is far, leading away beyond. What was the errand, what the commission? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā?
I roam as the sent messenger of Indra, seeking your great treasures, O Paṇis. A swift leap in fear helped us across—thus I crossed the waters of the Rasā.
What is Indra like, O Saramā, what does he look like—as whose messenger you have come from afar? Let him come here; we will make friendship with him; then let him be the lord of our cattle.
I do not know him as one to be deceived—he who would deceive, it will hit him—as whose messenger I came from afar. Deep flowing streams do not hide him; slain by Indra, O Paṇis, you shall lie.

title: Rigveda
text:
These are the cows, O Saramā, that you were seeking, flying around the ends of heaven, O fortunate one. Who would release these for you without fighting? And our weapons are sharp.
Not fit to be commanded are your words, O Paṇis; your bodies are not fit for arrows—let them be evil. Let the path for you be impassable; may Bṛhaspati not show mercy to you in either way.
This treasure, O Saramā, based in the rock, filled with cows, horses, and riches—the Paṇis guard it, those who are good herdsmen; you have come to a vain, empty step, O messenger.
The Ṛṣis shall come here, sharpened by Soma—Ayāsya, the Aṅgirasas, the Navagvas. They will share out this pen of cows—and then, O Paṇis, your words will vomit forth.
So then you have come here, O Saramā, driven by divine force. We will make you our sister; do not go back. We will give you a share of the cows, O fortunate one.
I know no brotherhood nor sisterhood; Indra knows it, and the terrible Aṅgirasas. The desire for cows concealed from me when I came—fly hence, O Paṇis, afar.
Go far away, O Paṇis—far away! Let the cows go forth, released by the sacred law. The cows that Bṛhaspati found hidden, and Soma, and the pressing stones, and the inspired Ṛṣis.
These were the first to speak about the Brahman's offence: the Boundless Ocean, the Waters, Mātariśvan, the Remover of the Firm, the fierce Tapas the bliss-giver, the divine Waters firstborn by the sacred law.
Soma the king was the first to restore the Brahman's wife, giving her back without anger. Varuṇa and Mitra were his followers; Agni the hotar led her taking her by the hand.
Her pledge should be taken by the hand alone—'this is the Brahman's wife,' so they said. She is not to be sent to a messenger; thus the realm of the Kṣatriya is protected.
The gods of old spoke about this matter, and the seven Ṛṣis who sat down to austerity: the wife brought home of a Brahman is terrible; she brings an evil condition in the highest heaven.

title: Rigveda
text:
The Brahmā-student wanders, pouring out poison; he becomes a single limb of the gods. By means of him Bṛhaspati found again his wife who had been led away by Soma—like the gods the ladle.
The gods gave her back again; and humans too gave her back. The kings, acting in truth, gave the Brahman's wife back again.
Having given back the Brahman's wife, having removed the offence together with the gods, they worship the wide-stepping one, having partaken of the nourishment of the earth.
Kindled today in the house of Manu, O Jātavedas, as god you worship the gods. Come and bring them, O friend of Mitra, discerning one; you are the messenger, the sage, the all-knowing.
O Tanūnapāt, anointing with honey those who travel the paths of sacred law, making them sweet, O fair-tongued one—perfecting our thoughts with prayers and the sacrifice—make our oblation reach the gods.
Being invoked, worthy of praise and worship—come, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus. You are the youngest Hotṛ of the gods; being sent, you most fit to sacrifice—worship them.
The sacred grass is strewn facing east, spread at the point of this abode at the beginning of the days. It spreads out broader and wider, a soft seat for the gods and for Aditi.
Let the spacious ones spread themselves wide, adorning themselves like wives for their lords. O divine doors, broad and all-filling, be good entrance ways for the gods.
The two who flow fair and are worshipped nearby—let Night-and-Dawn sit down in their womb, the two divine maidens, tall and well-adorned, assuming the bright, white-gleaming splendour.
The two divine Hotṛs, the first, the fair-voiced, measuring out the sacrifice for man to worship—inspiring the two artisans at the assemblies, directing the eastern light according to the quarter.
Let Bhāratī come swiftly to our sacrifice; let Iḷā awaken here in the manner of Manu; let the three goddesses—Sarasvatī, the skilful-working ones—sit on this comfortable sacred grass.

title: Rigveda
text:
He who fashioned all the worlds with forms—him, these two parents Heaven and Earth—worship here today, O Hotṛ, sent and most fit to sacrifice, knowing it—the god Tvaṣṭṛ.
Release of yourself, anointing, setting the oblations in their season upon the path of the gods—let the tree, the slaughterer, and the divine Agni make the offering savoury with honey and ghee.
Born at once, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the forerunner of the gods. In the direction of this Hotṛ, in the voice of the sacred law, let the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā.
Bring forth your wisdom, O wise ones, in accord with the thoughts that dwell in men. With true and mighty acts let us impel Indra — for he is the hero, the lover of song, the knowing one.
The thought from the seat of Ṛta blazed forth; the bull, son of Gārṣṭi, roared with the cows. He rose up with his mighty war-cry and spread himself through the vast realms of space.
Indra alone, it is said, knows this by hearsay; for he is the conqueror, the pathmaker for the Sun. Making the slope traversable, the unshaken one became lord of the cow, lord of heaven, ancient, unapproachable.
Indra, praised by the Aṅgirases, with his greatness overthrew the vow of the great ocean. He who has stretched out the many realms upholds the firm foundation of truth and reality.
Indra knows the measure of heaven and earth; he slays Śuṣṇa at all the soma-pressings. He stretched out even the great sky with the Sun; the great prop himself propped it up with a prop.
For Vṛtra-slayer smote Vṛtra with the vajra and the magic spells of that ungodly, bellowing one. There, O bold one, you slew boldly; and thus, O Maghavan, you became mighty-armed.
When the Dawns joined with the Sun, his rays found that wondrous lustre. When the asterism appeared like the sky's own light, no one truly knows whence it came again.

title: Rigveda
text:
Far, indeed, those foremost waters went — they that flowed forth at Indra's impulse. Where was their source, where their bottom? Where, O waters, is your middle now, where your end?
You released the rivers swallowed by the serpent; straightway these rushed forward with speed. Whether still seeking release or already released, these sharp-edged ones still do not rest.
United, yearning, like eager ones they came to the river; from of old the lover, the destroyer of strongholds, was roused for them. O Indra, the earthly riches went homeward; many gracious bounties came to us.
O Indra, drink your fill of the pressed soma — the morning-pressing is yours as first draught. Rejoice, O hero, to smite your enemies; we proclaim your heroic deeds with hymns of praise.
Come with that chariot of yours, O Indra, swifter than thought, to drink the soma. Let your tawny horses run swiftly — those with whom you travel, the bulls, rejoicing.
Touch your body with the tawny splendour and radiance of the Sun, with the finest forms. Being invoked by us your friends, O Indra, sit down and rejoice in our company.
Whose greatness in exaltation these two great worlds, Heaven and Earth, have not encompassed — come with your beloved tawny horses yoked, O Indra, to your home, toward the beloved food.
He whose enemies you have ever slain with incomparable heroic deeds in battle — he sings of your mighty power; for him, O Indra, this pressed soma is for your exhilaration.
This your ancient bowl, O Indra — drink the soma with it, O you of a hundred powers. The ladle is full of the sweet inebriating drink that all the gods wholly desire.
In many ways do the peoples call upon you, O Indra, O bull, when they have set out their offerings. Let these pressings of ours, sweetest for you, be among those you love, O lord.

title: Rigveda
text:
Of you, O Indra, I now proclaim the ancient heroic deeds, the first that were done. With your fury unabated you cleft the rock and made the cow easy to win for the worshipper.
Sit down among the hosts, O lord of hosts; they call you the most inspired of poets. Without you nothing whatsoever is accomplished from afar. O Maghavan, sing the great, wondrous hymn.
Look down upon us suppliants, O Maghavan; be mindful, O lord of wealth, friend of friends. Make battle, O maker of battle, with your true strength — even those who share not, do grant us a share in riches.
Heaven and Earth, of one mind with all the gods, assisted his energy. When he went forth making his Indra-power great, having drunk of the soma, he grew in wisdom.
Viṣṇu, bounding forward with might, proclaims his greatness and the power of the soma-stalk. Indra, the bountiful, together with the united gods, slaying Vṛtra, became supreme.
When bearing weapons he stood face to face with Vṛtra the serpent to fight, making known his prowess — then all the Maruts together in their own might, O fierce one, increased your Indra-greatness.
Even at birth he repelled his rivals; the hero looked forward to the manly battle. He split the rock, let the grain fall, released the waters; with his skill he propped wide the vault of heaven.
Straightway Indra claimed all mighty powers for himself; he pushed aside the broad Heaven and Earth. The bold one brought down the iron vajra as a boon to Mitra and Varuṇa, the bountiful.
Then, before his mighty powers — the vigorous, roaring ones — they yielded to his wrath. When the fierce one clove Vṛtra mightily with his power, the waters that had been held wrapped in darkness were released.
The heroic deeds first to be done — as the two strove together with their greatnesses — when the darkness of gloom was laid low and slain, Indra leaped forth in his greatness at the first invocation.

title: Rigveda
text:
Then all the gods increased your manly powers with praise and with the eloquence that the soma inspires. Vṛtra the serpent who had been overcome by Indra's blow, fire separated his joints like food for the eager one.
With many powers, with eloquent verses, with friendship proclaim the friendship. Indra, who deceived Dhuṇi and Cumuri, listens with trusting heart to Dabhīti.
Bring us many goods with good horses, whereby, reciting the proper utterances, you may approve. May we pass through all difficulties by easy paths; find for us today the wide shallow ford.
The two hot milk-vessels spread on all sides the threefold; Mātariśvan came to take pleasure in them. The gods, seeking the milk of heaven, found the hymn mighty with its thousand.
The three Nirṛtis wait upon the guardian; the priests know them who have heard from afar. The sages have discerned their source — those that are in the secret vows of the higher ones.
The young woman of four braids, beautifully adorned, wears before her face ghee and the ordinances. In her two strong eagles settled — there where the gods established their portions.
One eagle entered the ocean; he surveys this entire world. I saw him with a simple mind from nearby — the mother licks him, and he licks the mother.
The inspired poets speak of the one eagle with their words, and fashion him in many ways. They establish the metres at the sacrifices and measure the twelve soma-cups.
Fashioning thirty-six plus four, and establishing the metres up to twelve — the sages measuring out the sacrifice in their wisdom drive the chariot forward with Ṛc and Sāman.
Fourteen are the greatnesses of this one; the seven wise ones guide him with speech. Who here would declare the far-reaching ford, by which path they drink up the pressed soma?
The fifteen praises in a thousandfold — as far as Heaven and Earth extend, so far is that. Thousandfold the greatnesses, a thousand — as far as brahman is spread, so great is speech.

title: Rigveda
text:
What wise one knows the yoking of the metres? Who has attained the word directed to the bright one? Who, they say, is the eighth heroic priest? Who really has discerned the two tawny horses of Indra?
Some roam about the ends of the earth; they stand on the shafts of the chariot, yoked. Among these they distribute the share of fatigue when Yama is placed in the dwelling.
Wondrous indeed is the growth of this young child who does not go to his two mothers to suckle. If he was born uncollected, yet straightway he grew; running his great messenger's course at once.
Agni has been established by name, the most eager at giving — he who binds the forests together with his tooth of ash. Sweeping forward with his tongue in perfect sacrifice, like a bull snorting over fodder.
Him — the divine bird who pecks at the wood, the drop of soma snorting and pouring forth his flood — him, blazing like a carrier-priest with his flame, of mighty vow, like one whose rays run along the paths.
Of your ageless, glowing advance, the unshaken winds are not around like those of a burning-arrow. The eager ones, like eager fighters, attain Trita as their guide and go forward for seeking.
He is indeed the Agni most dear to the Kaṇvas, friend of the Kaṇvas, the noble overcoming lord of the utmost interior. May Agni protect the singers, may Agni protect the patrons, may Agni grant us their favour.
For the most prize-winning, the conquerable, of good father — for Jātavedas restless and stirred — even he who boldly claims the boon of the waterless one, for the most exalted, who stretches his bow, seeking to shoot.
Thus Agni, the good one, son of strength, is praised along with mortal patron-lords and men — like allies who are well-established and devoted to Ṛta; like bright heavens they are over men with their brilliance.

title: Rigveda
text:
Grandson of Strength, O you mighty with power — so speech, the bull, praises you being worshipped. We will laud you; with you may we be rich in heroes, establishing ever longer life to extend further.
Thus, O Agni, the sons of Vṛṣṭihavya, the ṛṣis, have spoken in their praise. Protect both them and the patron-lords who hymn you — they reached upward with 'vaṣaṭ vaṣaṭ', they reached upward with 'namo namaḥ'.
Drink the soma for great Indra-power, drink, O mightiest, to slay Vṛtra. Being invoked, drink for wealth and strength; drink the sweet draught, O Indra, be satisfied and rain down blessings.
Drink of this, of the abundant, the forthcoming — drink, O Indra, the choicest of the pressed soma. With a well-being-granting mind rejoice, turning toward prosperity for the sake of good fortune.
May the heavenly soma delight you, O Indra; may that which is pressed on earth delight you. May that whereby you made abundance delight you; may that whereby you destroy enemies delight you.
Let Indra of twofold might, the bull, come eagerly to the soma poured out with his two tawny horses. In the bowl of the pressed and offered sweet juice, rain benefits all at once, O friend of the red cows.
Sending the sharp and glittering weapons flashing down, make firm the power of those sped by sorcerers. I give you strength and might against the fierce foe; in the retreats hack the enemies to pieces.
O Indra, spread widely your glories; stretch your strength like a taut bowstring against the attackers. Growing in power on our side, unstoppable, do you yourself grow strong in body.
This oblation is given to you, O Maghavan; accept it, O universal king, without disdain. For you is the soma pressed, for you it is ripened, O Maghavan — eat and drink, O Indra, of the forthcoming offering.
Indeed eat, O Indra, these oblations that are set forth; take pleasure in them and cook the soma. Offering gifts, we are eager to win your favour; may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled.

title: Rigveda
text:
I send forth my eloquent praise to Indra and Agni, driving it like a boat on the river with hymns. Like spokes the gods go around — those who give wealth to us and are givers of discoveries.
Verily the gods have not decreed that hunger alone shall be death; even though a man is full, death can still reach him. Yet the wealth of one who gives does not diminish, and the one who gives not finds no comforter.
