He who, having food, hardens his heart toward the needy person, hungry and wretched who has come to him — though he cultivated him before, he finds no comforter.
He indeed is the true enjoyer who gives to the wandering indigent, to the hungry and lean. He becomes fit for the call-to-aid, and even in future things he makes a friend.
He is no friend who gives nothing to his friend, his companion who goes along with him — one should depart from such a one; there is no dwelling with him; let one seek another who gives, even if a stranger.
The stronger man should give to the supplicant; let him look ahead to the longer road. For riches roll around like chariot wheels; they come to one man after another.
The foolish man gets food in vain — I speak truth — that is his death. He neither nourishes Aryaman nor a friend; he who eats alone, his sin is his alone.
The ploughshare ploughing brings reward; one who goes the road gains advantage through his journeys. The speaking Brahmin surpasses the one who speaks not; the giver who is an ally excels the non-giver.
One-footed surpasses two-footed in many ways; the two-footed approaches the three-footed from behind. Four-footed comes at the call of the two-footed, seeing the ranks, standing by.
Even two equal hands do not produce equally; even two identical twin cows do not give the same milk. Even twins are not equal in their powers; even two kinsmen do not give equally.

title: Rigveda
text:
O Agni, shining brilliantly, you slay the devourer among mortals, in your own home, O you of pure ordinance.
Well-kindled, you rise up and rejoice at the ghee when the ladles are set around you.
Summoned, Agni, who is to be praised with song, shines forth; his face is anointed with the ladle.
Agni is anointed with ghee, honey-faced, when oblations are given; he shines forth, rich in light.
As you blaze, growing old in your brightness, O carrier of oblations to the gods, mortals call upon you.
Mortals tend him, the immortal Agni, with ghee — the inviolable lord of the house.
With your inviolable flame, O Agni, burn the Rakṣas; shine forth as guardian of Ṛta.
You, O Agni, with your countenance burn back the sorceresses; shine forth in your wide dwelling.
Him you, the carrier of oblations, dweller in wide spaces, the most worthy of sacrifice among the human folk, they have kindled with songs.
So indeed is my mind: 'I would win a cow, I would win a horse' — have I drunk of the soma?
Like rushing winds, the draughts I have drunk have lifted me up — have I drunk of the soma?
The draughts have lifted me up, like swift horses a chariot — have I drunk of the soma?
Inspiration has come to me like a lowing cow to her beloved calf — have I drunk of the soma?
Like a carpenter rounding a chariot-body, I shape my thought in my heart — have I drunk of the soma?
The five peoples have not pleased me even a little — have I drunk of the soma?
Not even both the worlds, Heaven and Earth, equal even one of my wings — have I drunk of the soma?
In my greatness I have surpassed the sky; I have surpassed this great Earth — have I drunk of the soma?
Well then! Shall I set down this Earth here or there? — have I drunk of the soma?
I shall strike the Earth to a cinder, here or there — have I drunk of the soma?

title: Rigveda
text:
One of my wings is in heaven; I have dragged the other one down below — have I drunk of the soma?
I am the greatest of the great, raised up to the very clouds — have I drunk of the soma?
I go home, well-equipped as the bearer of oblations to the gods — have I drunk of the soma?
That was the greatest thing in the worlds: from it was born the fierce one of dazzling might. As soon as born he destroys enemies; all his helpers rejoice after him.
Growing in power, of many energies, he plants terror in the heart of the Dāsa enemy. Both the unshot and the shot arrow he won; your offered gifts are praised in the exaltations.
All fold their purpose into you when these helpers become twice and thrice more. Sweeter than sweet, mix the sweet together; fight that sweetness indeed with the honey of honey.
For thus the inspired ones exult after you, winning riches, exaltation by exaltation. Stretch yourself firm and mightier, O bold one; may the ill-doing sorcerers not deceive you.
With your help we have prevailed in battles, beholding many things worth fighting for. I urge your weapons with my words; with prayer I sharpen your powers.
I would praise the one of many forms, the skilled one, the most overpowering, the Āptya among the Āptyas. He shatters the seven streams with his might; he overcomes many and matching things.
You hold fast both the lower and the upper; in whose house you have protected with your shelter — you establish the two mothers as they come, and from there you dispatch many heroic deeds.
These prayers Bṛhaddiva, the foremost, the heaven-winner, proclaims as his praise-shout to Indra.
Thus great Bṛhaddiva the Atharvan declared himself to be Indra himself. The stainless sister-winds that breathe on the mother-streams urge him on and increase him with their might.
Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; born, he was the one lord of all that exists. He sustained this earth and yonder heaven. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?

title: Rigveda
text:
He who gives breath, who gives strength, whose command all things obey, whose command even the gods obey — he whose shadow is immortality and whose shadow is death. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
He who, by his might, became the sole king of every breathing, every winking thing — he who is lord of this two-footed and four-footed world. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
He whose greatness these snow-capped mountains proclaim, whose they say the ocean is, together with Rasā — whose are these four directions, whose are the arms. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
By whom the awesome sky and the earth were made firm, by whom heaven was propped up and the vault of light — who is the measurer of the midspace. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
To whom the two armies trembling in mind looked up for help, propped up by his aid — above whom the sun shines when it has risen. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
When the mighty waters came, bearing the universal germ, generating Agni — from that was born the one breath of the gods. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
He who by his power looked over the waters as they held creative force and generated sacrifice — he who was the one god above the gods. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
May he not harm us — the father who brought forth the earth, who, upholding truth, generated the sky, and who generated the bright, mighty waters. To which god shall we render worship with oblation?
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these born beings. May whatever desire of ours we invoke you for be granted; may we become lords of riches.
I praise him who is like a good treasure, of wondrous greatness — the pleasant, auspicious, inoffensive guest. He, Agni the hotar, the householder, the sustainer of all, bestows on the devout the gift of heroic strength.

title: Rigveda
text:
O Agni, of wise will, pleased, accept and love my words, you who know all the ways. Clothed in ghee, open the path of prayer; the gods followed after your ordinance.
The immortal one, traversing the seven stations, bestows on the generous, the pious — be gracious to us. With wealth that brings good heroes, O Agni, self-existent, be pleased with him who has served you with fuel.
Those with oblations praise the foremost ensign of sacrifice, the purohita, the seven-powered. Agni who listens, whose back is anointed with ghee, the bull, the god who satisfies — bestows heroic strength on the giver.
You are the first and most excellent messenger; invoked, rejoice for immortality's sake. The Maruts purified you in the house of the generous worshipper; the Bhṛgus made you shine bright with their praises.
Milking refreshment from the easily milked cow that nourishes all, O sacrifice-loving Agni of wise will, for the sacrificer — dripping ghee, shining thrice through the ritual seasons, going round the sacrifice, you seek wisdom.
You alone, at the shining forth of this Dawn, men making you their messenger have worshipped. The gods increased you, worthy of great praise, anointing you with ghee at the sacrifice.
The Vasiṣṭhas called you down, O swift one, praising you, O Agni, wise ones, at the assemblies. Establish the flourishing of wealth among the sacrificers. You gods, ever guard us with your blessings.
This Vena has set in motion the speckled-bellied one, the light-wombed, the measurer of the midspace. The inspired ones caress with their thoughts this one here, at the meeting of the waters with the sun, as they would a young child.
Vena the sky-born raises a wave from the ocean; the back of the tawny one, the beloved, is seen. Shining on the peak of cosmic order, dwelling in the heights, the bands sang forth together toward the common womb.

title: Rigveda
text:
Many, crying out toward the same one, they stand — the mothers of the calf, nestled together. Stepping forward on the peak of cosmic order, they lick the voices of the sweet and immortal one.
The inspired ones, knowing his form, cried out; for they went toward the sound of the gazelle, of the buffalo. Going by the law of cosmic order they stood upon the stream; the Gandharva found the immortal names.
The Apsaras, smiling at her lover, the woman, bears him in the highest heaven. Moving in the wombs of the beloved one, he who is himself beloved — that Vena sits upon the golden wing.
When they beheld you flying toward the vault of heaven, with their hearts longing they gazed upon you — the golden-winged bird, messenger of Varuṇa, the active bird in the womb of Yama.
The Gandharva stood upright upon the vault of heaven, carrying his variegated weapons turned outward. Wearing a fragrant garment to behold — like the sun he generated dear names.
The drop that moves toward the ocean, viewing with the eagle's eye the one who holds apart — the sun, gleaming with bright radiance, placed dear things in the third sphere of the firmament.
Come to this our sacrifice, O Agni — the five-staged, triple, seven-threaded. Be our carrier of oblations and our vanguard. For too long indeed you have lain in the long darkness.
From the non-divine I go as a god by the expansive hidden path, seeing before me immortality. That which is auspicious — though inauspicious I abandon — I go from my own friendship to a stranger-navel, a new home.
Seeing the guest of another, the bird, I measure out the many stations of cosmic order. I declare what is beneficial to our father Asura; I go from the unworthy of sacrifice to the portion worthy of sacrifice.
Many years I spent within this one; choosing Indra, I leave behind my father. Agni, Soma, Varuṇa — they are set in motion. That kingdom has been turned back; I seek to protect it as it comes.

title: Rigveda
text:
Those Asuras have lost their magic powers, and you, O Varuṇa, desire me. O king, separating truth from falsehood — come to sovereignty over my kingdom.
This is the heavenly light; this indeed was the prize; this is the illumined, the wide midspace. Let us two smite Vṛtra — come forth, O Soma! You are the oblation; we worship you who are such with oblation.
The seer, by his seer-power, has fixed his form in heaven; Varuṇa, by his unobstructed might, released the waters. Like women, like rivers making a home, those shining ones continually carry his color.
They accompany his greatest power; rejoicing in their own nature they dwell with him. Choosing him as their king, as clans choose a ruler, the loathers stood away from Vṛtra.
The yoke-companion of those who loathe, the swan moving in fellowship with the celestial waters — the seers knew Indra to be of anuṣṭubh meter, roaming after it, echoing it again and again, through wisdom.
I move with the Rudras and the Vasus; I move with the Ādityas and the Viśvadevas. I bear both Mitra and Varuṇa; I bear Indra and Agni, and I bear both Aśvins.
I bear Soma the crusher, and I bear Tvaṣṭṛ, and Pūṣan and Bhaga. I bestow wealth on the one who offers oblation, on the sacrificer who presses Soma and is worthy of aid.
I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures, the discerning one, foremost among those worthy of worship. The gods distributed me in many places — I who have many abodes, who enter into many things.
Through me, whoever sees, whoever breathes, whoever hears what is spoken — eats food. Those who do not know me dwell beside me. Hear, O you who are heard! I speak to you what is worthy of trust.
I alone speak this, beloved of gods and of men alike. Whomsoever I love, that very one I make mighty — I make him a brahman, a seer, a person of great wisdom.

title: Rigveda
text:
I stretch the bow for Rudra, that his arrow may slay the hater of sacred knowledge. I make battle for the people; I have entered into heaven and earth.
I give birth to the father of this world upon its summit. My womb is in the waters, within the ocean. From there I spread through all the worlds, and with my greatness I touch yonder sky.
I myself blow like the wind, embracing all the worlds. Beyond the sky and beyond this earth — such is my greatness; I have become.
No distress, no sin has touched that mortal, O gods, whom Aryaman, Mitra and Varuṇa lead in agreement past his enemies.
For that very thing we choose you, O Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman — by which you guard and lead the mortal free from distress, past his enemies.
May those — Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman — now come here for our aid. The most skilled guides shall guide us on our going; the best ferriers shall ferry us across, past our enemies.
You protect the whole world — Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman. May we be in your dear shelter, well-guided, past our enemies.
The Ādityas — Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman — pass beyond those who slip. We invoke fierce Rudra with the Maruts, and Indra and Agni, for our welfare, past our enemies.
Be leaders then for us across — Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman — past all mishaps, kings of humankind, past our enemies.
May Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, grant us abundant aid — may the Ādityas of wide renown grant shelter for what we seek, past our enemies.
Just as you, O Vasus, O adorable gods, once freed even the aurochs-cow that was bound by the foot — so now release us from distress! O Agni, stretch our life forward, still farther.
The divine Night, arriving, has looked forth in many places with her eyes. She has put on all glories.
The immortal goddess has filled the wide depths and the heights. With her light she drives away the darkness.

title: Rigveda
text:
The goddess, arriving now, has indeed sent away her sister Dawn. And now the darkness too retreats, withdrawing.
She, at whose passage today we have settled down as birds settle into a tree to their dwelling — to that one be propitious to us.
The villages have settled down, the creatures with feet have settled, and so too the birds — even the eagles, intent on their prey.
Keep away the she-wolf and the wolf, keep away the thief, O Ūrmī — and then be easy for us to pass through.
The darkness, thick and palpable, has crept up and enveloped me. O Dawn, like a debt, make it pay and depart.
I have approached you as cattle approach — accept it, O daughter of heaven; receive this praise-song, O Night, as one who has won the prize.
May my brilliance be present, O Agni, in the manifold invocations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies. May the four quarters bow down to me; with you as our overlord, may we conquer in battles.
May all the gods be in my invocation — the Maruts with Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni. May the midspace and the wide realm be mine; may the wind blow for me in this desire.
May the gods sacrifice wealth into me; may blessing be upon me, may the invocation of the gods be upon me. The divine hotars of old sought to win — may we be unharmed in body and rich in heroic sons.
Let them sacrifice for me; may the intent of my oblation be true to my mind's purpose. May I not fall into any sin whatever — let all you gods speak in my behalf.
Make the six divine spacious realms wide for us; all you gods, show your heroic power here! May we not lose progeny or bodies; may we not fall into the power of him who hates us, O King Soma.
O Agni, warding off the fury of our enemies, inviolable guardian, protect us! May their hidden foes go back again; may their wakened thought come to naught.

title: Rigveda
text:
May Dhātṛ the establisher, lord of the world, the divine protector who overcomes assailants — may both Aśvins, Bṛhaspati, and the gods guard this sacrifice and the sacrificer from harm.
May the great bull of wide reach grant us shelter in this invocation — the much-invoked, the much-possessing one. O Indra of the bay steeds, be merciful to us for our progeny; do not harm us, do not abandon us.
Let our rivals be away from us; we press them down with Indra and Agni. The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas have made the fierce, all-knowing overlord to reach on high.
Then was neither non-being nor being; there was neither the realm of space nor the sky beyond. What stirred? Where? In whose shelter? Was there water, the deep and unfathomable?
Death was not then, nor immortality; no signal was there of night and day. That One breathed, windless, by its own power; other than that, nothing whatsoever existed.
Darkness was hidden by darkness in the beginning; all this was undifferentiated water. The life-force that was covered with emptiness — that One arose through the power of heat.
Desire came upon That One in the beginning — that which was the primal seed, born of the mind. The seers, searching within their hearts with wisdom, found the bond of being in non-being.
Their cord was stretched across — was it below? Was it above? There were seed-placers; there were powers. Self-sufficiency below, impulse above.
Who truly knows? Who here shall proclaim it? Whence was it born? Whence came this creation? The gods came after the creation of this world — who then knows from where it arose?
He from whom this creation arose — whether he made it or whether he did not — he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he alone knows — or perhaps he does not know.
The sacrifice that was spread on all sides with threads — the one-hundred-and-one, extended by the acts of the gods — these fathers who came as weavers now sit weaving at the web, crying 'Weave on, weave on.'

title: Rigveda
text:
A man extends it; a man cuts it up; a man has spread it out upon this vault of heaven. These pegs have taken their seat together — they have made the sāmans the shuttle-bobbins for the weaving.
What was the measure? What was the model? What was the fastening? What was the ghee? What was the enclosure? What was the meter? What was the introductory chant? What was the recitation — when all the gods sacrificed to the god?
Agni was joined to the Gāyatrī; Savitṛ came together with the Uṣṇih meter; Soma, great with anuṣṭubh recitations, was yoked to them; Bṛhaspati's Bṛhatī covered speech.
The Virāj is the glory of Mitra and Varuṇa; the Triṣṭubh is Indra's portion of the day here. The Jagatī entered into all the gods; with that the seers and human beings were made fit.
The seers and human beings were made fit by that, when the sacrifice was born, our fathers of old. With the mind's eye, I think I see those who first performed this sacrifice.
Together with the praise-songs, together with the meters bound together, together with the measures — the seven divine seers. The wise ones, looking back along the path of the ancients, grasped the reins like chariot-drivers.
Drive away from us, O Indra, O conqueror, all enemies toward the east, drive them toward the west; drive them toward the north, drive the mighty ones downward, that we may rejoice in thy broad shelter.
Do those who have barley indeed thresh the barley in order, one after another? Make the enjoyments of those here and here [for us], who have not come [merely] to bend the knee at the sacred grass.
Not by the proper season is the [fitting] time of your coming, nor has renown been found in assemblies — the inspired poets, desiring cattle, desiring horses, seeking the stallion Indra for friendship.
You two Aśvins, while drinking the surā with the Asura Namuci, O lords of splendour, having drunk deeply, helped Indra in his deeds.

title: Rigveda
text:
Like two parents [guarding] a son, you two Aśvins aided Indra with your wisdom and wondrous powers. When thou drankest the surā in full with thy might, Sarasvatī, O bountiful one, sprinkled thee.
May Indra, the good protector, self-sufficient with his aids, all-knowing, be gracious to us. May he thrust back enmity, make us fearless — may we be lords of heroic vigour.
May we be in the good favour and the blessed benevolence of that worshipful one. May that Indra, the good protector, self-sufficient, drive enmity far away from us, even from afar.
Heaven, rich in good treasure, blessed the sacrificer; Earth, the abundant bestower, [blessed] the sacrificer. The two divine Aśvins caused the sacrificer to thrive with their favours.
You two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, supporters of the settlements, we worship, urged on by your great favour. May we, through friendship with you twain, be beyond the reach of demons.
Even now, as we strive toward you with the dear wealth that we cherish — or as the wealth he has given thrives — none [can] dispute his bounties.
That other [sky] was born as a heaven, O Asura; thou, O Varuṇa, art king of all. The head of the chariot so chosen — not so great a guilt does a sin-destroyer [demand].
In this [friend], truly, O Śakapūta, this guilt [lies]: one kills the heroes who are bound in Mitra held fast. Or what benefit he established in their own bodies, in those dear to them and sacred to the sacrifice.
For Aditi, your mother, all-wise, has purified [you both] with her milk, like Heaven or like Earth. [Now] shine down, beloved ones; the Sun has anointed [you] with his rays.
For you two, kings of possession, were seated in the standing chariot, resting on the shaft, sitting in the forest. May those [helpers], roaring for us — Nṛmedhas saved us from trouble; Sumedhas saved from trouble.

title: Rigveda
text:
Sing forth a mighty [hymn] to Indra, with the pūroratham [verse] first. Even in close combat a world-maker, in encounters and in battles a slayer of Vṛtra — be our inciter. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
Thou didst release the rivers flowing downward, thou didst slay the serpent. O Indra, thou wast born without enemies; thou dost nourish all that is desirable — thee we embrace. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
May all the hostile ones perish; may those of the enemy not harm our prayers. Thou art the hurler of the slaying bolt against the foe who would kill us, O Indra; thy bounty gives wealth. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
Whoever of the people around us, O Indra, points out [the way] with the eye of a wolf — bring him down low; thou art the repeller, the conqueror. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
Whoever harms us, O Indra, whether he be of our own kin or a stranger — overcome his strength, as great Heaven does by its own power. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
We, O Indra, yearning for thee, take hold of friendship. May he lead us by the path of Ṛta beyond all evils. May the bowstrings of the others snap on their bows.
Do thou, O Indra, generously grant us that [cow] who yields according to the wish of the praiser — may the great cow with a thousand streams, with unbroken udder, pour milk upon us.
When thou, O Indra, didst fill both the world-halves, like the Dawn — the divine mother brought thee forth, great, emperor of the great ones, sovereign of the peoples; the auspicious mother brought thee forth.
Pierce through the stubborn [body] of the mortal who is ill-intentioned toward us; bring low him who points [enemies] at us — the divine mother brought thee forth, the auspicious mother brought thee forth.

title: Rigveda
text:
Shake down those great refreshments, bright as all things, O slayer of enemies; with thy powers, O Śakra, O Indra, with all thy aids — the divine mother brought thee forth, the auspicious mother brought thee forth.
When thou, O Indra of a hundred powers, shakest all things down, together with riches for the soma-presser, with a thousandfold of aids — the divine mother brought thee forth, the auspicious mother brought thee forth.
Let the missiles fall in all directions around like drops of sweat; may ill-will depart from us like the threads of the dūrvā grass — the divine mother brought thee forth, the auspicious mother brought thee forth.
For thou bearest the goad like a long hook, O thoughtful one; with thy former step, O bountiful one, thou dost direct the people like Yama — the divine mother brought thee forth, the auspicious mother brought thee forth.
We do not injure the gods; we do not obstruct [their worship]; we walk [the path of] obedience to the sacred word. Here, with wings and with embracing arms, we together take hold [of you].
In the tree with beautiful leaves where Yama drinks with the gods — there our father, the lord of the dwelling, delights in the ancient ones.
I gazed after him, the one who follows after the ancient ones, walking along the evil path; grieving, I yearned for him once more.
The new chariot without wheels which thou, O boy, didst fashion in thy mind — it has but a single shaft, facing all sides: thou climbest upon it unseen.
The chariot thou, O boy, didst set rolling beyond the wise sages — that [chariot] rolled on together with [the hymn]; a boat was set on [the voyage].
Who begat the boy? Who set the chariot rolling? Who could today tell us how the gift-for-the-dead came to be?
As the gift-for-the-dead came to be, from that the beginning was born. The foundation was spread out in front; behind, the exit was made.

title: Rigveda
text:
This dwelling of Yama, which is called the god-built hall — here his flute is blown, here he is adorned with songs.
The Keśin bears fire; the Keśin bears poison; the Keśin bears heaven and earth. The Keśin bears all to behold the sun; the Keśin is called this light.
The munis are girdled with the wind; they wear soiled [garments] of yellowish-brown hue. They follow the rushing course of the wind, wherever the gods have vanished.
Exhilarated by the state of the muni, we have mounted the wind. You mortals behold only our bodies.
He flies through the mid-air; he has seen all forms. The muni is the friend placed [as companion] for the good work of every god and every god.
The steed of the wind, the companion of Vāyu — the muni is impelled by the gods. He dwells upon both oceans, the eastern and the western.
Roaming in the footsteps of the Apsarasas, the Gandharvas, and the beasts — the Keśin, knowing [all] intentions, is the sweetest and most intoxicating friend.
Vāyu churned [the drink] for him; Kunannamā pounded it. The Keśin drank from the cup of poison when he drank together with Rudra.
O gods, what is cast down, the gods lift up again. O gods, even one who has committed sin, the gods restore to life again.
These two winds blow, from the Sindhu and from the far distance. May one blow vigour to thee; may the other blow away whatever disease [there is].
Blow hither the healing, O Wind; blow away the disease, O Wind. For thou art the universal healer; thou movest as the messenger of the gods.
I have come to thee with blessings, also with protections from harm. I have brought thee auspicious vigour; I drive away disease from thee.
May the gods protect him here; may the host of the Maruts protect him. May all beings protect him, so that he may be free from harm.
The Waters are indeed healers; the Waters dispel disease. The Waters are the remedy for all — may they work healing for thee.

title: Rigveda
text:
With both hands, the ten-branched ones, and the tongue that leads speech — with those two free-from-disease [hands], we touch thee with them.
Those bearers of oblation in thy friendships, O Indra, pondering the sacred order, burst Vala apart — where, honouring the Dawns and releasing the waters, [thou didst act] for Kutsa's praise, with thy wondrous deeds against the serpent.
Thou didst release the springs; driving forward, thou didst push away the mountains; thou didst drive up the bright [cows], thou drankest the dear sweet drink. Thou didst magnify the forests with his wonder; the Sun blazed with the hymn born of sacred order.
The Sun released his chariot in the mid-sky; the Ārya found a match for the Dāsa. The strongholds of Pipru the Asura, the deceiver — Indra burst them apart, acting together with Ṛjiśvan.
The irresistible one violently burst apart the irresistible [things]; Ayāsya crushed the god-less hoards. Like the Sun [taking] the communal wealth of the month, being praised he shattered the enemies with his gleaming [power].
Ayuddhasena, by the widespread [Indra] who cleaves, [the enemy] was granted [defeat]; the slayer of Vṛtra hones his sharp weapons. The crusher trembled at Indra's bolt; Śundhyu strode forth; the Dawn abandoned her car.
These are thy renowned [deeds], solely thine own, when one by one thou madest them offer no sacrifice. Thou didst place the ordering of the months in heaven; the father carries the wheel-rim split by thee.
Savitṛ with golden locks has raised up his light ceaselessly from the east. Pūṣan, knowing, goes forth at his impulse, the herdsman beholding all the worlds.
He, the beholder of men, stands in the mid-sky, having filled the two world-halves and the mid-air. He gazes all around at the luminous [regions], between the eastern and the western brightness.

title: Rigveda
text:
The foundation of wealth, the meeting-place of riches — he beholds all forms with his powers. Like the god Savitṛ of true ordinance, like Indra, he has not halted in the battle for treasures.
The Waters who had seen Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva, the Soma — they departed by sacred order. Indra, pleased, tracked them; he looked around at the enclosures of the Sun.
May Viśvāvasu, the heavenly Gandharva who measures out the firmament, sing that for us. Whether it be the truth, or whether we know it not — may he, spurring our thoughts, protect our thoughts.
He found the winning one at the course of the rivers; he opened the doors of the rocky enclosures. The Gandharva declared the immortal [words] to them; Indra came to know the power of the serpents.
O Agni, great is thy fame; thy flames blaze, O Vibhāvasu. O Bṛhadbhānu, with thy might thou bestowest the prize worth hymning upon the worshipping sage.
With purifying splendour, with bright splendour, with undiminished splendour thou risest with thy light. Moving about as a son [between] his two mothers, thou dost approach and fill both Heaven and Earth.
O grandson of Strength, O Jātavedas, rejoice with our fair praises, gladdened by [our] devotions. In thee the many-formed ones, of various refreshments, born of bounty, have gathered together their impulses.
Ruling, O Agni, O immortal, spread thyself widely through living beings among us as [bringer of] wealth. Thou shinest with radiant form; thou dost fill the winning purpose [with vigour].
Thou bestowest the great, auspicious gift of bounty and impulse with winning wealth — thou, the all-wise performer of the sacrifice, the sovereign of great munificence.
Men have placed Agni foremost for [their] welfare — the great bull, obedient to sacred order, visible to all, the one who hears [prayer]. With song, O divine one, the generations of men [praise] thee, the most widely renowned, whose ear is open.

title: Rigveda
text:
O Agni, speak here toward us; turn to us with favour, be well-disposed. Bestow gifts upon us, O Lord of the clan — for it is thou who art the giver of wealth to us.
May Aryamā bestow gifts upon us, may Bhaga, may Bṛhaspati; may the gods bestow, and also Sūnṛtā — may the divine lady of riches give to us.
We invoke King Soma for our aid, and Agni with our songs; the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Brahmāṇaspati.
Indra-and-Vāyu, and Bṛhaspati — we invoke them here with easy invocation, so that every person in the assembly may be well-disposed toward us.
Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to bestow gifts; urge Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Savitṛ, the impeller of prizes.
Do thou, O Agni, increase our prayer and sacrifice with thy fires; do thou impel the gods to come and wealth to be given to us.
This praiser, O Agni, O son of strength, has become dependent on thee — there is indeed no other refuge. For thy shelter is threefold and beneficent; keep far from us the gleam of those who would harm.
Thy birth is on the downward slope, O Agni, as thou seekest nourishment; like a companion thou dost embrace all beings. Let our seven hymns go forward and win prizes; they move in front, of their own accord, like a keeper of cattle.
Or thou dost devour all around with thy devouring mouth, O Agni of the thicket — thou who art self-sustaining; and the clumps become the cleared fields of the fertile tracts. May we not have provoked thy terrible missile.
When thou dost devour going over heights and into hollows, thou dost advance in different directions like an insatiable army; when the wind blows with thy blazing, thou dost shave the land, as a barber shaves the beard.
His ranks are seen all facing one single way; many are the chariots pursuing the single course. When, O Agni, smoothing thy arms along, thou dost search the upturned earth, bending downward.

title: Rigveda
text:
Let thy vigour rise up, let thy flame rise up, let the prizes of thee, O Agni, who hast laboured, rise up; rear thyself up and bow down as thou growest — today let all the Vasus take their seat in thee.
This is the downward course of the waters, the resting-place of the ocean; make for thyself another path from here — along that path go thou following the cows.
On thy coming-path and going-path, may flowering Dūrvā grasses grow; and ponds with lotuses — these are the houses of the ocean.
That Atri, made old by truth, swift to the goal as a horse to be driven — even Kakṣīvant, do ye two renew him as if making a chariot new.
Him, like a vigorous horse whom the particles of dust had covered — do ye two loosen the firm knot; bring Atri, made most young again, into the light.
O most wonder-working heroes, resplendent ones, ye two are eager to win hymns for Atri; and now, O men of heaven, a praise-song goes to you in turn for your renown.
That gift of yours and that good-will is conspicuous, O Aśvins of rich bounty — when, O heroes, ye carry us through in the wide assembly-place of our gathering.
Ye two brought Bhujyu, who had been tossed beyond the sea, to the farther shore of the realm of cloud; come hither with winged steeds, O Nāsatyas, made ready for the winning.
O most bountiful ones, knowing all things, come to us with your blessings, like beneficent spirits; adorn us, O heroes, with refreshments swelling like a spring.
This immortal drop, O Indra, speeds like a swift horse; this is the power, the all-sustaining life, for the ordainer.
This is the wise, Ṛbhu-like, the thunderbolt for the pious worshipper; this bears the exhilaration that makes the hairs stand erect — like Ṛbhu, the exhilaration wrought with skill.
Eager, practised for the falcon, going to its own proper haunts; it has shone down — the one that incites the serpent-slayer.

title: Rigveda
text:
That which the fair-winged one — the son of the falcon — brought from the distant region: the one of a hundred circles, the track of the serpent.
That which the falcon brought to thee with its foot, the lovely, harmless, ruddy measure of the Soma plant — by this, the life-giving power extends over life and living; by this, kinship keeps its vigil.
Thus, O Indra, with the drop, even among the gods, the great vigour is maintained; through wisdom the life-giving force extends over life, O wise one — through wisdom this has been pressed out from us for thee.
I dig up this plant, the most powerful of herbs, by which one drives away a rival wife, by which one wins a husband.
O plant with spreading leaves, O auspicious one, propelled by the gods, O powerful one — blow my rival wife away; make my husband mine alone.
I am the higher, I am higher, I am yet higher than the highest; and the rival wife who is mine — she shall be the lower, lower than the lowest.
I do not even take her name, nor does that person take delight in her — we shall drive the rival wife to the very farthest distance.
I am the conquering one, and thou art the utterly vanquishing one; both of us, having become conquering women together, let us overcome my rival wife.
I have placed the conquering one upon thee; I have overpowered thee with one yet more conquering. May thy mind run after me as a cow after her calf, as water runs along its path.
O Forest Goddess, O Forest Goddess — thou who seemest to vanish in the distance — why dost thou not ask after the village? Does no fear come upon thee?
When the cicada sings in answer to the bell-calling bull, the Forest Goddess is exalted, as if driving on with bells.
It seems as if cattle are grazing; it seems as if a dwelling is visible; and in the evening the Forest Goddess releases, as it were, the sound of creaking carts.

title: Rigveda
text:
Here one hears a cow being called; here someone has cut wood; one who dwells in the forest at evening thinks he has heard a shout.
The Forest Goddess does not slay anyone unless some other comes upon her; having eaten of the sweet fruit, she lies down at will.
Fragrant with collyrium-scent, sweet-smelling, rich in food, not ploughing — I have praised the Forest Goddess, the mother of wild beasts.
I place my faith in thy foremost fury, in that day when thou, O manly one, didst cleave Vṛtra and release the waters; when both the worlds trembled at thy vigour, O Indra, and even the earth shook at thee who wearest the stone.
Thou, O blameless one, with thy magic powers didst crush Vṛtra the magician by the mind that seeks glory; thee indeed do warriors choose in contests for cattle, thee in all desirable sacrificial rites.
Be gladdened, O much-invoked Indra, among these patrons — the thriving ones who, O Maghavan, have attained to bounty; they worship thee the prize-winner in contests for children and offspring, in winning of Soma, in shameless pursuit of wealth.
He indeed is delighted by the wealth well borne, who perceives the swiftness of it; O Maghavan, he who has grown strong through thee, whose sacrifice is offered, quickly wins the prize and riches through heroic men.
Being praised with greatness for the bold troop, make wide space, O Maghavan — be capable of giving riches; thou art our friend, O wonderworker, like Varuṇa the wise; like the food-allotter, thou art gracious in distributing.
We who have pressed the Soma and have won the prize praise thee, O Indra of mighty powers; bring us the bounty in which thou art pleased — aided by thee, may we win it with body and offspring.
Thou art exalted, O hero Indra, born to overcome the Dāsa folk with the Sun; we carry the hidden, secret thing concealed in the waters, as the Soma in a flowing stream.

title: Rigveda
text:
Or let the inspired sage, knowing the words of the seers, sing out hymns for thee, desiring thy favour; may we be among those who rejoice thee with Soma draughts, yoked to thee, O chariot-rider, with their shares.
These prayers, O Indra, I offer to thee — give heroes' heroic power to the men, O hero; be of one mind with those in whom thou art pleased, and protect both the singer and the women.
Hear the spacious call, O hero Indra, and thou art praised with the hymns of the desirable one; those floods that rush like tidal waves into thy ghee-filled birthplace, making it gleam.
Savitṛ fixed the earth with supports; Savitṛ propped the sky without a pillar; he milked out the restless atmosphere as if a horse; Savitṛ bound the ocean that is unfathomable.
Where the braced ocean spread out, Savitṛ, the Son of the Waters, knows of it; from thence the earth arose, from thence the bright space arose, from thence Heaven-and-Earth expanded.
Afterwards there came into being the other sacred thing — by the abundance of the immortal world; the fair-winged Garuḍa was born before Savitṛ himself, and he follows even Savitṛ's law.
As cattle come to the village, as the fighter to the horses, as a lowing cow, milking sweetly, to the calf — may Savitṛ, all-desirable upholder of heaven, come to us like a husband to his wife.
O Savitṛ of the golden pillar, as Aṅgiras invoked thee for this prize — so, worshipping and praising thee for aid, I am wakeful toward the shoot of Soma.
Though already kindled, thou dost kindle thyself afresh as the bearer of oblations to the gods; come to us with the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus — come to us for our welfare.
Rejoicing in this sacrifice and this speech, come near; we mortals invoke thee, O thou who art kindled — we invoke thee for our welfare.
Thee, O Jātavedas, thee all-desirable, I praise with my prayer; O Agni, bring to us the gods of beloved rites — for our welfare, those of beloved rites.

title: Rigveda
text:
Agni became the divine priest of the gods; the human sages have kindled Agni; I invoke Agni in the great contest for wealth — for welfare, for the winning of wealth.
Agni aided Atri, Bharadvāja, and Gaviṣṭhira; he aided Kaṇva and Trasadasyu in battle; Vasiṣṭha, the divine priest, invokes Agni — for welfare, as divine priest.
By Śraddhā (Faith) Agni is kindled; by Śraddhā the oblation is offered. I proclaim Śraddhā at the head of Bhaga (the Bountiful Lord), with my voice.
O Śraddhā, make dear the one who gives; make dear the one who desires to give. Make this utterance of mine dear among the generous and among the sacrificers.
Just as the gods placed Śraddhā in the Asuras and in the mighty ones, so make our utterance dear among the generous and among the sacrificers.
The gods and the worshippers, guarded by Vāyu, attend upon Śraddhā. By Śraddhā, by the sincere resolve of the heart, one obtains riches.
Śraddhā we invoke in the morning; Śraddhā we invoke at midday; Śraddhā we invoke at the setting of the sun. O Śraddhā, cause us to have faith here.
Thus command, thou who art great, the miraculous devourer of enemies. He whose friend is never slain and never in any way overcome.
May Indra, the lord of the people, the giver of welfare, the slayer of Vṛtra, the subduer of enemies, the mighty bull, the drinker of soma, the bestower of fearlessness, go before us.
Drive away the Rakṣas; drive away the oppressors; smash the jaws of Vṛtra. Drive away, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, the wrath of the enemy who attacks us.
Drive away our oppressors, O Indra; press down the assailants. He who attacks us — send him down to the lower darkness.
Drive away, O Indra, the mind of the hater; drive away the blow of him who seeks to overcome us. Grant the shelter of thy grace; keep away the weapon afar.

title: Rigveda
text:
They who are active, swinging, attend on newly-born Indra; they have attained heroic strength.
Thou, O Indra, wast born with surpassing strength, from might and vigour. Thou, O bull, art indeed the bull.
Thou, O Indra, art the slayer of Vṛtra; thou didst extend the atmosphere apart. With thy might thou didst prop up the sky.
Thou, O Indra, bearest in thy arms the hymn along with the dawn, whetting the vajra with thy might.
Thou, O Indra, art the overpowerer of all beings with thy might. Thou hast become the lord over all existing things.
For some Soma flows purified; for others ghee is attended upon; for those for whom honey streams forth — to them verily may this one (the deceased) go.
Those who by austerity are invincible, those who by austerity have gone to heaven, those who have made great austerity — to them verily may this one go.
The heroes who fight in battles, who give up their bodies, or those who bestow a thousand sacrificial fees — to them verily may this one go.
Those who first of all served the cosmic order, the guardians of ṛta, the promoters of ṛta — O Yama, send this one to those ascetic Fathers; to them verily may this one go.
Those seers of a thousand paths who guard the sun — O Yama, may this one go to those ascetic ṛṣis, to those born of tapas.
O one-eyed, disfigured Arāyī (niggardly demon), go to the mountain without a path. With the warriors of Śirimbiṭha do we drive thee away.
Driven hence and driven thence, O red one who destroys all embryos — O Lord of prayer (Bṛhaspati), come here with sharp horns, looking at the Arāyī (niggardly demoness).
That piece of timber which floats yonder on the other bank of the river, uninhabited by men — seize it, O evil-natured one; with it cross over to the farther shore.
Those who came from the east, the maṇḍūradhāṇikīḥ (dealers in iron-rust), all the enemies of Indra were slain, swift as bubbles.

title: Rigveda
text:
They have led the cow around me; they have carried the fire around; among the gods they have won fame. Who now shall dare attack this woman?
Let our prayers urge Agni on like a swift horse in the races; by him may we win wealth upon wealth.
O Agni, by that army of thine, under thy protection, with which we have gathered cattle — urge that on for us to gain wealth.
O Agni, bring us abundant, wide-spreading wealth, rich in cattle and in horses; fill the well; turn away the Paṇi (miser).
O Agni, cause the ageless star, the sun, to rise in the sky, bearing light for mankind.
O Agni, thou art the banner of the clans; thou art the most beloved, the best who is present. Be aware of the singer; grant him vigour.
May Indra and all the gods now fulfil these worlds for us.
May Indra together with the Ādityas arrange for us the sacrifice, our bodies, and our progeny.
May Indra, together with the Ādityas and in company with the Maruts, be the protector of our bodies.
When the gods came, having slain the Asuras, guarding their divine sovereignty —
— they brought back the sun-hymn (the light) with their powers; and thereupon they beheld the vigorous self-law (svadhā, the primordial order of the universe).
May the Sun protect us from the sky; may Vāyu (the Wind) protect us from the atmosphere; may Agni protect us from earthly dangers.
O Savitṛ, thy golden arm is worthy of a hundred impulsions (savā). Protect us from the falling lightning.
May the divine Savitṛ grant us sight; may the mountain grant us sight; may Dhātṛ (the Creator) bestow sight upon us.
Grant us sight for the sake of seeing; grant us sight for beholding, for our bodies. May we together look out and see around us.
May we look upon thee, O Sūrya, beautiful in appearance. May we behold thee, endowed with vision like men.

title: Rigveda
text:
Yonder sun has risen; this my good fortune (bhaga) has risen. I, who am wise and ever-victorious, have overcome my husband entirely.
I am the banner; I am the head; I am the powerful one who speaks out. My husband shall follow my will; let him attend upon me who am victorious.
My sons are slayers of enemies; my daughter is a ruling queen. I myself am all-conquering; and my praise is supreme among my husband's people.
With that oblation by which Indra performed his deed and became supremely resplendent — O gods, by that have I become free from rivals.
Rival-free, slayer of rivals, victorious and overpowering — I have seized the lustre of those others as if seizing the wealth of those who offer nothing.
I have conquered these rivals of mine, I who am the overpowerer; so that I may reign supreme over this hero and over his people.
Drink of this sharp and invigorating draught; release both thy bay horses here, O all-conquering one. Let not other worshippers turn thee away, O Indra; these soma-pressings are for thee.
For thee are these pressed drinks; for thee too are the soma-pressings; the praises of the assembly call thee hither. O Indra, delighting in this pressing of today, knowing all things, drink the soma here.
He who with eager mind, with whole heart, devoted to the gods, presses soma for Indra — his cattle Indra does not give away to another; he makes for him a praiseworthy and pleasing (outcome).
He is left to suffer who, though wealthy, does not press soma for Indra. The bountiful Indra lays him down in misfortune; he slays the hater of sacred prayer, himself unbidden.
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, desiring booty, we call thee, that thou shouldst come to us. Seeking favour in thy new grace, may we call thee, O Indra, for happiness.
I release you with oblation for the sake of life, from the unknown consumption and from the royal consumption (rājayakṣma). If the Grāhī (the seizing demon) has seized him, from her, O Indra and Agni, set this one free.

title: Rigveda
text:
Whether his life-span is exhausted, whether he has already departed, whether he has been led to the very threshold of Death — I bring him back from the lap of Nirṛti; I have rescued him for a hundred autumns.
With the thousand-eyed oblation that brings a hundred autumns and a hundred years of life, I have fetched him back — that Indra may lead this man through a hundred autumns, beyond all misfortune.
Live a hundred autumns, growing in strength; live a hundred winters, a hundred springs! May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati restore this man again with an oblation that bestows a hundred years of life.
I have brought you back; I have found you; you have come again, renewed. O whole-limbed one, all your sight have I found for you, and all your life-span.
May Agni, the slayer of demons, acting in concert with sacred prayer (brahman), drive away from here the disease called Amīvā, of evil name, that lies lurking in your womb and endangers your embryo.
That Amīvā of evil name which lies lurking in your womb threatening your embryo — Agni together with brahman has driven out that flesh-eating demon.
Him who kills the (embryo) that flies about, that settles in the womb, that creeps — him who seeks to destroy the child once born — that one we drive away from here.
Him who forces apart your thighs when husband and wife lie together, who licks inside the womb — that one we drive away from here.
Him who, having become as a brother or a husband, or as a lover, lies down upon you — who seeks to destroy your offspring — that one we drive away from here.
Him who, having deluded you through sleep and darkness, lies down upon you — who seeks to destroy your offspring — that one we drive away from here.
From your eyes, from your nostrils, from your ears, from your chin — the head-disease (śīrṣaṇya yakṣma) from your brain and from your tongue — I tear it out for you.

title: Rigveda
text:
From your neck, from your nape (uṣṇihā), from your vertebrae (kīkasā), from the spine (anūkya) — the shoulder-disease (doṣaṇya yakṣma) from your shoulders and from your arms — I tear it out for you.
From your intestines, from your rectum, from the vaniṣṭhu (belly-region), and from above your heart — the disease from your kidneys (matasnā), from your liver, from your spleen — I tear it out for you.
From your thighs, from your knees, from your heels, from the balls of your feet — the disease from your hips, from the buttocks, from the hinder parts — I tear it out for you.
From the organ of urination, from the groin (vanaṁkaraṇa), from your body hair, from your nails — the disease from your entire self — this one I tear out for you.
That which has arisen from limb to limb, from hair to hair, from joint to joint — the disease from your entire self — this one I tear out for you.
Depart, O lord of the mind; step away, go far off! Speak of the manifold mind of the living man from beyond Nirṛti (Dissolution).
Auspicious indeed is the boon they choose; auspicious is the right hand they yoke. Auspicious is the eye of Vaivasvata (Yama); manifold is the mind of the living man.
Whatever wrong we have incurred through hope, through imprecation, through slander, while awake or while asleep — may Agni place all evil deeds, all things displeasing, far away from us.
O Indra, O lord of sacred prayer, whatever treachery we commit — may the wise Āṅgirasa guard us from the sin of enemies.
We have conquered today; we shall conquer; we have become free from sin. The evil of waking thought and dreaming, of evil intention — let it befall him whom we hate; let it befall him who hates us.
O gods, this dove, sent purposefully and desiring something, has come here as a messenger of Nirṛti (the goddess of ruin). For him let us sing and perform the rite of expiation. May there be welfare for our two-footed (creatures), welfare for our four-footed (creatures).

title: Rigveda
text:
May the dove sent (as an omen) be auspicious to us; may the bird be free of sin in our houses, O gods. May Agni, the wise one, accept our oblation; may the winged shaft (of Nirṛti) turn away from us.
May the winged shaft not harm us; it places its foot on the fire-holder (āṣṭryā). May there be welfare for our cattle and our people; may the dove not injure us here, O gods.
What the owl cries — that is in vain; and what the dove's foot touches in the fire. He whose messenger this one has been sent — to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage.
With the Ṛc (verse) drive away the dove, drive it off; exulting in refreshment, lead the cow around. Having closed off all evil, let the most excellent one fly forth, abandoning his strength for us.
Make me the bull among equals, the one who overcomes rivals, the slayer of enemies, the sovereign (virāj), the lord of cattle.
I am the slayer of rivals, unharmed and uninjured like Indra. These rivals are all trodden down beneath my feet.
Right here I tie you (rivals) together, as both ends (of a bow) are tied by the bowstring. O lord of speech, silence these men so that they may speak beneath me.
I have come as the overpowering one, with the power of Viśvakarman. I take possession of your minds, your vows; I take possession of your assembly.
Having taken your welfare and prosperity, may I become the highest; I have stepped upon your heads. Speak up to me from beneath my feet, as frogs (croak) up toward the water, as frogs (speak) from the water.
For you, O Indra, this sweet liquor is poured out; you reign over the pressed (soma) and the jar. Grant us wealth with many heroes; through fervent ardour you have won the heavenly light (svar).
We call upon the mighty, greatly exhilarating, heaven-winning (Soma), around the mighty Śakra (Indra) where it is pressed. O be aware of our sacrifice here, come hither; we beseech the bountiful one (Maghavan) who is victorious in contests.

title: Rigveda
text:
In the ordinance of King Soma and of Varuṇa, with the approval of Bṛhaspati, in his shelter — in your praise today, O Maghavan, O Dhātṛ, O Vidhātṛ, I have drunk the jars (of Soma).
Urged on, I have taken my share; I have partaken of the food; I, the first sage, polish up this hymn of praise. If with the pressed (Soma) and with (the prize) won I have come to the house of you two — Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni.
Now the greatness of the Wind's chariot — its sound goes crashing and thundering; it touches the sky, turning all things ruddy, and it goes stirring up the dust of the earth.
Along with (the Wind) the troops of the Vātasya (Wind's hosts) rush together; the women go toward him like (going to) an assembly. Yoked together with them, on the same chariot, this god travels — the king of this whole world of beings.
Traveling through the middle air by his paths, he does not rest in any place on any day. The firstborn friend of waters, the guardian of cosmic order (ṛtavan) — where indeed was he born? From whence did he come to be?
The breath (ātman) of the gods, the embryo of the world — this god moves as he wills. His sounds alone are heard, not his form. To that Vāta (Wind) let us offer homage with oblation.
May the bliss-giving Wind blow upon (the cows); may the vigorous plants satisfy them. May the fat-uddered ones, bringing life in their grain, drink; O Rudra, show grace to the quadruped for the good of the settlement.
Those (cows) of like form, of differing form, of one form — those whose names Agni knows by sacred rite — those which the Aṅgirasas employed here for penance: to them, O Parjanya, grant great shelter.
Those (cows) that have displayed their bodies among the gods, all of whose forms Soma knows — those, swelling with milk for us, rich in offspring — let them flow, O Indra, in the cow-stall.

title: Rigveda
text:
Prajāpati, having gifted these to me, acting in accord with all the gods and ancestors — auspicious as they are, has led them into our cow-stall. Together with their offspring may we sit down with them.
Let the great Resplendent One (Sūrya) drink the sweet Soma-beverage, placing unimpaired life in the lord of the sacrifice. Urged by the Wind, he who guards (creation) by his own power — he has nourished creatures and shines widely in manifold ways.
The great Resplendent One, well-borne, most winning of prizes, established in truth on the foundation of heaven's ordinance — the slayer of non-allies, slayer of Vṛtra, most potent slayer of Dasyus — this light was born, slayer of Asuras and of rivals.
This is the best of lights, the highest light; called the Great, the all-conquering, wealth-conquering. Sūrya — the all-illumining, great in splendour, great to behold — has spread widely together with unfaltering might.
Blazing with light, the sun went to the shining realm (svar), to the luminous realm of heaven — that (light) by which all these worlds are upheld through the all-doing (Viśvakarman), protected by all the divine powers.
You, O Indra, saved that chariot of the one who pressed Soma, the one who had been forced away; you heard the call of the Soma-presser.
You cut off the head of Makha who was shaking violently, you stripped him of his skin; you went to the house of the Soma-presser.
You, O Indra, repeatedly loosen that mortal man, Vena, beloved, from the one who has an arrow-shaft at his base, for the one who is eager in mind.
You, O Indra, caused that sun, which was behind, to come to the fore, even against the will of the gods.
Come hither together with the forest; the cows follow the track with their udders.
Come hither with a treasure-bringing thought, O most munificent one who kindles Makha, with thy bountiful gifts.

title: Rigveda
text:
Like those sustained by nourishment, we who are bountiful set on the thread; we worship.
Uṣas rolls away the darkness of her sister, she rolls the track well by her noble birth.
I have brought thee hither; abide among us, stand firm, unmoved and unshaken. May all the peoples desire thee; may the kingdom not fall away from thee.
Be here, do not depart; stand firm here, unmoved like a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra; hold fast the kingdom here.
Indra has made him firm with the firm oblation; Soma has spoken for him, and for him the Lord of Prayer has spoken.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm are these mountains; firm is all this world; firm is this king of the peoples.
May King Varuṇa make thee firm, firm the god Bṛhaspati; may Indra and Agni hold firm thy firm kingship.
With the firm oblation we touch Soma to make him firm; moreover, may Indra make the peoples, all of them, tribute-bearers to thee.
With the all-surrounding oblation with which Indra compassed all about, with that, O Lord of Prayer, turn us round for kingship.
Surpassing the rivals, surpassing those who are our enemies, stand thou over the one who fights against us, over him who hates us.
God Savitṛ has encompassed thee round about, Soma has encompassed thee; all beings have encompassed thee so that thou art the all-surrounding one.
By which oblation Indra, having acted, became most glorious — with this the gods have wrought it: I have indeed become one without a rival.
Without rivals, a slayer of rivals, all-encompassing, overpowering adversaries — so that I may rule over all these beings and over the people.
May god Savitṛ impel you forward, O pressing stones, according to the ordinance; be yoked in the shafts, press out the Soma.
O pressing stones, drive away ill-omen, drive away evil intent; you who are like the rays of dawn, make healing.

title: Rigveda
text:
The pressing stones, setting about the upper ones in unison, glorify themselves; they bestow on the bull his virile power.
May god Savitṛ now impel you, O pressing stones, according to the ordinance — for the sacrificer who presses.
Loudly the sons of the Ṛbhus shout forth; the settlements exult, they who are all-sustaining on the earth, who have drunk from the cow as from a mother.
With a divine thought bring forward the god Jātavedas; may he carry our offerings in unbroken succession.
This one here who is pious, the Hotṛ, is led forth for the sacrifice; like a well-harnessed chariot he who is full of warmth moves by his own impulse.
This Agni rescues as if from immortality at birth; stronger even than strength, the god is made for the sake of life.
The wise ones behold with heart and mind the bird anointed by the Asura's magic power; the seers discern him within the ocean, and the inspired ones seek the track of the rays.
The bird carries Speech in his mind; the Gandharva uttered it within the womb. The seers guard that shining, heavenly wisdom at the station of the Ṛta.
I saw the Herdsman who never alights, going hither and thither on his paths; clothed in garments that converge and that go in all directions, he moves round and round within the worlds.
Let us invoke here for our well-being that prize-horse Tārkṣya, spurred by the gods, victorious in battles, conqueror of chariots, with unbroken felloes, a champion in battles, swift.
Calling aloud for Indra's gift of bounty, let us mount him for our well-being as a boat; on the wide, broad, deep expanse — may we not be harmed in our going, nor in our return.
He who at once with his might spread the five peoples like the sun with light — his speed that wins thousands, that wins hundreds, does not withdraw from a young woman or an arrow.

title: Rigveda
text:
Rise up, both of you, look upon Indra's seasonable share; if it is cooked, pour the libation; if uncooked, be ye gladdened.
The oblation is cooked — come forth, O Indra; the sun has gone to the mid-point of the path. Thy companions sit around thee with treasures, as herd-keepers around a leader of the troop as he goes.
I deem it cooked in the udder, cooked in the fire; I deem that truth the newest and best. Drink, O Indra wielder of the vajra, much-doing, enjoying gladly the curds of the midday pressing.
Thou hast overcome the enemies, O Much-invoked; may thy might be supreme, thy generosity here. O Indra, bring wealth with thy right hand; thou art lord of the rich rivers.
Like a fearsome beast that roams the mountains, thou hast come hither from the far-off distance beyond. Sharpening thy sharp blade and bolt, O Indra, strike the enemies asunder, thrust aside the battles.
O Indra, thou wast born with might and lordly power, O bull of the tribes; thou didst thrust away the people who acted as enemies, and madest a wide space for the gods.
Whose name is Pratha and Sapratha — the oblation of the Anuṣṭubh, the offering of that offering — from Dhātṛ the resplendent, from Savitṛ and from Viṣṇu, Vasiṣṭha brought forth the Rathaṃtara Sāman.
They found what had been hidden away — the supreme seat of sacrifice that lay in secret: from Dhātṛ the resplendent, from Savitṛ and Viṣṇu, from Agni, Bharadvāja fashioned the Bṛhat Sāman.
Meditating with the mind, they found the spilled Yajus verse — the first, the path of the gods — from Dhātṛ the resplendent, from Savitṛ and Viṣṇu; these ones brought the gharma (the hot-milk oblation) down from the Sun.
May Bṛhaspati lead us through the difficult passes; may he not guide thought toward the evil-tongued again. Driving away the curse, smiting malevolence, may he then make wellbeing and peace for the sacrificer.

title: Rigveda
text:
May Narāśaṃsa protect us at the fore-oblation; may there be well-being for us at the after-oblation, in our invocations. Driving away the curse, smiting malevolence, may he then make wellbeing and peace for the sacrificer.
He of the burning head — let him scorch those rākṣasas who hate the sacred word and deserve the arrow of slaying. Driving away the curse, smiting malevolence, may he then make wellbeing and peace for the sacrificer.
I saw you with the mind, wide-awake, born of tapas, manifested through tapas; bestowing offspring here, bestowing wealth here — come forth with progeny, O you who desires a son.
I saw you with the mind, meditating, yearning in your own body in the season's time; may the young woman come up to me — come forth with progeny, O you who desires a son.
I placed the embryo in the plants; I dwell within all the worlds. I have engendered offspring upon the earth; I have given sons to mothers thereafter born.
Let Viṣṇu prepare the womb; let Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms; let Prajāpati pour the seed; and let Dhātṛ, the ordainer, establish the embryo in you.
Place the embryo, O Sinīvāli; place the embryo, O Sarasvatī; may the two divine Aśvins, garlanded with lotuses, place the embryo in you.
The golden fire-drill which the two Aśvins churn together — that embryo we invoke for you, to be brought to birth in the tenth month.
Great and heaven-abiding be the aid of the three — of Mitra and of Aryaman — and irresistible the protection of Varuṇa.
Neither at home, nor on the roads, nor in the mountain strongholds does the evil-minded foe, the evil-tongued, hold sway against them.
For that mortal to whom the sons of Aditi extend the unceasing light, that he may live.
Let the Wind blow its medicine — bringing ease, bringing bliss — to our heart; may he prolong our spans of life.

title: Rigveda
text:
And you, O Wind, are our father, and our brother, and our friend — make us live.
That which yonder, O Wind, in your house has been laid up as a store of immortality — from that, grant us life.
Send forth your voice to Agni, the bull of the peoples; may he carry us across and beyond the hostile.
He who shines forth across the far distance, across the desert wasteland — may he carry us across and beyond the hostile.
He who, the bull, drives back the rākṣasas with his bright and pure flame — may he carry us across and beyond the hostile.
He who gazes out over all the worlds and beholds them together as one — may he carry us across and beyond the hostile.
The bright Agni who was born on the far shore of this realm of space — may he carry us across and beyond the hostile.
Urge forward now Jātavedas, the steed, the swift one — to take his seat upon this our sacred kuśa grass.
Of this Jātavedas, the inspired hero, the bountiful bestower, I send forth the great and excellent praise.
With those bright flames of Jātavedas that carry the oblation to the gods — with those may he impel our sacrifice.
This dappled cow has stepped forward; she has settled before her mother and proceeds toward the father — toward the heavenly light.
Within the luminous vault she moves, breathing in and out from his breath; the great bull has illumined the sky.
Thirty stations shine resplendent; speech is directed toward the winged one (the Sun); at each of the two twilights, day by day, through the luminous days.
From blazing tapas, cosmic order (ṛta) and truth (satya) were born; from that, night was born; from that, the billowing ocean arose.
From the billowing ocean the year was born; he who is master of all that blinks and breathes ordained the days and nights.
Dhātṛ, the ordainer, established the Sun and Moon as they were before — heaven and earth, the mid-space, and the realm of celestial light.

title: Rigveda
text:
Together, altogether you kindle all things, O bull, O Agni, O Lord; on the seat of Iḷā you are kindled together — bring to us all good things.
Come together, speak together; let your minds be in agreement. As the gods of old, in concord, partook of their appointed share — so may you.
Common is the counsel, common the assembly, common the mind, and joined together the intention of these; with a common counsel I address you all; with a common oblation I make the offering to you.
Common be your purpose; common your hearts; let your mind be as one — so that all may go well for you together.
